title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
Prerequisites: Save Point (for git diff). Jupyter experience helps but is not required. Objective: explain why a one-line change to a notebook produces a noisy diff, and name four ways to make the change reviewable. Time: about 15 minutes.
Verified: ran diff and git diff --no-index --stat on the mock notebooks on 2026-11-16 (macOS, Python 3.9.6). Tool facts: Last verified (docs, not run): nbformat, nbstripout, jupytext, nbdime and marimo docs on 2026-11-16.
Files: before.ipynb and after.ipynb, two tiny mock notebooks (about 2.5 KB each). They are mock files: they omit cell ids, so they are not strictly valid nbformat 4.5. Save both into an empty folder.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
section: A notebook is a JSON file
text:
A notebook is a JSON file
A .ipynb file is a JSON document with metadata, nbformat, nbformat_minor (the notebook file-format version numbers) and a list of cells. A code cell stores its source, but also an execution_count and its outputs. A plot is stored inside the file as a base64 string (the image bytes written out as plain text). The format keeps source and outputs in the same file, so any run rewrites lines next to the code.
Whether you use an agent or not, this is what git sees. The two mock notebooks differ by one real change: the cutoff 30 became 40. Compare them:
diff before.ipynb after.ipynb
5c5
<    "execution_count": 3,
---
>    "execution_count": 7,
8c8
<     "print(len([r for r in reads if r >= 30]))"
---
>     "print(len([r for r in reads if r >= 40]))"
15c15
<       "3\n"
---
>       "2\n"
21c21
<       "image/png": "AAECAwQFBgcICQoLDA0ODxAREhMUFRYXGBkaGx...
---
>       "image/png": "AAMGCQwPEhUYGx4hJCcqLTAzNjk8P0JFSEtOUV...
Four changed spots, one of them is the code. The rest is the run counter, the printed result and an image blob. General practice, not measured here: in a real notebook an image is often tens of kilobytes on a single line, and there are usually many cells. The format docs describe the structure; that this makes diffs noisy is our reading of it, and the output above is the evidence.
The risk with a coding agent is the same as with a human: a reviewer who cannot find the code change will approve without reading it.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
section: Four ways to make changes reviewable
text:
Four ways to make changes reviewable
Each of these is one option among several. Each moves the noise somewhere else.








Option
What it does
Cost




nbstripout
Strips outputs and some metadata when git stores the notebook. Outputs stay in your working file, so on its own it does not change what an agent reads.
Git cannot set up the filter on clone, so each collaborator runs nbstripout --install themselves.


jupytext
Pairs the .ipynb with a .py (the py:percent format is recommended for code). You review the .py; outputs stay in the .ipynb.
Two files to keep in sync.


nbdime
A notebook-aware diff: nbdiff in the terminal, nbdiff-web in the browser, with git integration and a merge driver.
Everyone reviewing needs it installed.


marimo
Notebooks are stored as pure Python, so ordinary git diffs work.
A different notebook tool from Jupyter. marimo convert your_notebook.ipynb > your_notebook.py converts an existing one.



General practice: the costs above are our judgement, except the nbstripout clone limit, which is from its docs. Pick by what your team can adopt; stripping outputs is likely the smallest change and a different notebook tool the largest.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
Review the code cells
Whatever you choose, the review habit is the same:

Look at the source cells. Treat outputs as something to regenerate.
Run git diff --stat before committing and look for a notebook that grew by megabytes.
An output in a diff shows that something ran once; a re-run shows whether the code produces it.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
With a companion

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Claude Code reads a .ipynb with all its cells and outputs, and an output-heavy notebook fills context. It edits notebooks with NotebookEdit, one cell at a time, by cell_id. Replacing a code cell clears that cell’s execution count and saved outputs, so the agent’s diff in the notebook contains lost outputs as well as new source. Note that nbstripout is a git filter: outputs stay in the working file, so on its own it does not change what the agent’s Read returns. To keep the agent on the code, strip outputs from the working copy (nbstripout’s pre-commit mode modifies the working copy, per its docs) or point the agent at the paired .py. That is general practice; check the docs for your version.


The idea is the same: review the source cells. This quest has no tool-specific claims for OpenCode; check its docs for how it handles notebook files.

title: The Reviewer’s Code

Formats that review well
Notebooks are one example. A marimo notebook is stored as a plain .py file, so a diff shows what changed. A Jupyter .ipynb is JSON that also stores outputs and run counts, so diffs are noisy and hard to read, though stripping tools exist. If you ask an agent to produce analysis, prefer a format your reviewer can actually diff.

title: Send Small, Say So
text:
Prerequisites: Spot the Mirage. The Wall of Output is advised. Objective: hand work to collaborators, whether or not they use LLMs, without passing them your review burden. Time: about 15 minutes. General practice, not a vendor claim. Not checked: any venue’s disclosure policy. Team norms you agree locally override these defaults.
A reef is a community. When you use an agent, the cost of checking its output must not silently land on the next person. The Review-leech feeds on exactly that.
Four habits:
These help reviewers who use LLMs and those who do not. A colleague who does not use LLMs can review your work without learning a tool.

title: Send Small, Say So
section: When you worry about looking lazy
text:
When you worry about looking lazy
A common worry: people will think I am lazy or unoriginal for using it. You can make the facts easy to see.

Say plainly what the agent did and what you checked. “The agent drafted the plotting code. I read it and compared the output with a hand calculation.”
Follow your team’s norm. Some groups want a note in the commit message, some in the methods. Use what yours agrees on.
Let the evidence speak. Tests, checks and your ability to explain every line show the work is yours.
Ask. A lead or a journal editor can tell you what they expect.
Check the venue. Some venues have disclosure policies. If you name one, read its own page and cite it.

title: Boss: The Wall of Output
text:
Prerequisites: Ground Truth. This is the boss at the end of the trunk. Objective: survive a wall of agent output without reading all of it and without trusting all of it. Time: about 10 minutes. Each right answer on the first try damages the boss.
Practice guidance, not a vendor claim. Based on the habits taught in this zone.

title: Boss: The Wall of Output
text:
The Wall
The Wall is thousands of lines of generated diff (the list of lines a change added and removed), produced faster than anyone can review. If you merge it unread, the Blight spreads. If you try to read all of it, your attention thins and you approve things you did not understand. Both routes fail.
The way through is to refuse it whole: keep a review budget (only produce as much as you can honestly review today, because bulk low-quality output is called slop), ask for smaller pieces, ground each piece in a check, and pass on only work you have read yourself.
The AI for Science best practices (a European draft with no endorsements yet; practice 9) back this with a warning about the human check itself. Stating the human check is only the first step: oversight often fails through automation bias (trusting the machine’s output too readily) and rubber-stamping (approving without reading). Their example is an “approve each item” step at hundreds of items an hour, which turns into clicking through. A check that works shows what changed, at a volume a person can read, with approve, edit, veto and stop. They also say to keep a real decision point wherever results or other people are affected, and to record the human step as part of the work’s provenance. Not checked first-hand: read 2026-11-20 through a fetch summary, so re-check the wording on the page; see research/aiforscience.md.

title: Ground Truth
text:
Prerequisites: Spot the Mirage, a terminal with Python 3 and awk, and the two exercise files below (about 1 KB in total). Nothing here touches your own data. Objective: find out whether a script an agent called “tested” is actually right, using a check the agent did not write. Time: about 15 minutes.
Verified: ran gc.py and the awk check on 2026-11-13 (macOS, Python 3.15, Apple awk). Output below is the real output.
Files: tiny.fasta and gc.py. Save both into an empty folder.

title: Ground Truth
text:
The lantern
An agent gave you gc.py, which reports the GC content of each sequence, and said “tested, works”. Test it yourself:
python gc.py tiny.fasta
You should see:
seq1    50.0
seq2    20.0
seq3    25.0
Now measure the same thing a different way, with a tool the agent did not write. This awk command uppercases each line, counts G and C, and counts the total length:
awk '/^>/{if(n)print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"; n=substr($1,2); gc=0; t=0; next}
     {s=toupper($0); t+=length(s); gc+=gsub(/[GC]/,"",s)}
     END{print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"}' tiny.fasta
seq1    6 GC of 12 total
seq2    6 GC of 10 total
seq3    2 GC of 8 total
Work out the percentages and compare them row by row with the script. Two of the three rows tell a story, and one of them is not a bug at all. Then take the battle.

title: Ground Truth
text:
Say what the agent did
When agent work reaches a paper or a report, the AI for Science best practices (a European draft with no endorsements yet; practice 7) suggest a few habits. Make each answer traceable to its sources. Cite by persistent identifier (a permanent ID, such as a DOI for a paper or an accession number for a dataset), confirm that the identifier points to the real source, and then generate the reference from it with a tool that is not a language model, so a model does not write the reference text. Keep retraction status with the citation. Make clear what a person did and what an agent did, and disclose agent use where results are published. Record the model version, the inputs and the tool calls of each run (the record of where a result came from is called provenance) so you can look again later. You stay accountable for the judgement whatever the agent found. Their page also cites publisher and journal-editor policies (for example that an AI cannot be an author); check your target journal’s own rules, since we did not read those. Not checked first-hand: the practice page, read 2026-11-20 through a fetch summary, so re-check the wording on the page; see research/aiforscience.md.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
Prerequisites: Recruit the Beast. Adopt the Pet is advised, not required. Objective: set the model and the effort on purpose, especially when you hand work to a subagent, and learn to compare two settings on your own task. Time: about 15 minutes. The exercise is a worksheet and needs no model.
Last verified (docs, not run): research/model-and-effort.md sources on 2026-11-17; the model-config, effort, sub-agents, costs, choosing-a-model and optimizing-for-cost pages were spot-checked live that day; model names, aliases and defaults change often; Mistral Vibe and model pages read 2026-11-20 (research/mistral.md)
The companions in the Kennel are models; the tool around them (the harness, the program that runs the model and its tools) is the armour. This page is about which companion to bring to which job, and how hard to make it think. Model names, aliases and defaults change often, so check the current docs and your own tool before relying on any name here.
A few words first. A model tier is a size class of model: a smaller one is faster and cheaper, a larger one is more capable and costs more. An alias is a short nickname (such as sonnet) that the tool maps to a concrete model version. Effort is how much the model thinks before each step. A subagent is a helper the main agent starts with its own fresh context, which does a side task and returns only a summary. To delegate is to hand a task to a subagent. A token is a chunk of text, the unit that usage and cost are counted in, and context is the text the model can see right now. Frontmatter is the small settings block at the top of a Markdown file. To pin a model is to name one exact version so it never silently changes, and inherit means “use whatever the parent is using”. The prompt cache is a short-term store that makes re-reading an unchanged conversation cheaper.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
1. Two dials

Model is what the companion knows and can do.
Effort is how much it thinks per step. Lower effort means fewer and terser tool calls (the actions the agent takes, such as reading a file or running a command); higher effort means more thoroughness.

The docs say tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. One article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs: effort cannot add knowledge the model lacks, so a model that does not know an unusual method will not find it by thinking longer. Treat that as a hypothesis to test.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
2. How to set them

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Model. Aliases the docs list: default (clears an override and names no model), best (same as opus), fable, sonnet, opus, haiku, sonnet[1m], opus[1m] (the [1m] forms ask for a longer context window), and opusplan (the opus model in plan mode, then sonnet for the execution). Plan mode is a mode in which the agent proposes a plan and edits nothing until you approve it. On the Anthropic API the docs map opus, sonnet and haiku to the current 5.5 versions; other providers can resolve the same alias to older versions.








Way
How
Note




In a session
/model <alias or name>
alone, it opens a picker; Enter saves it as your default, s keeps it for this session only


Per launch
claude --model <alias or name>



Environment
ANTHROPIC_MODEL



Settings file
model field




For results that must be reproducible (a lab pipeline, course material), pin a full model name such as claude-opus-5-5, because an alias moves when a new version ships (our inference from how aliases work). The docs also offer ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL to pin what each alias means.
Effort. /effort, claude --effort, the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, or the effortLevel setting. The levels are low, medium, high, xhigh and max, and which ones exist depends on the model. The default differs by model and by surface. For Sonnet 5.5, the Claude Code model-config page says medium, while the API effort page says high on the API, so name the surface before quoting a default, and run /effort in your own tool to read yours.
Per skill and per subagent. Both skill files and subagent files take model and effort in their frontmatter.

A skill’s model takes the same values as /model, or inherit. A skill’s model and effort apply for the rest of that one turn and are not saved. A skill’s effort overrides the session level but not CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL.
A subagent’s model takes sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, a full model ID, or inherit. Its effort takes low to max. If the subagent’s model differs from the main one and you give no effort, the session level does not apply to it, so set it.
Which model a subagent gets, first match wins: the per-call model parameter, then the definition’s model, then the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL, then the main conversation’s model.

A subagent is a Markdown file with frontmatter in .claude/agents/ (project) or ~/.claude/agents/ (yours). Sketch, not run:
---
name: log-reader
description: Reads long pipeline logs and reports only failed tasks with their error lines.
model: haiku
effort: medium
---
Read the logs you are given. Return: task name, exit status, the first error line.
Quote lines exactly. If something is unclear, say so.
A subagent definition can also limit what the helper may use (a tools field): the sub-agents docs in Lore below give the exact syntax, which this sketch leaves out.
Why medium? The docs say Haiku 5.5 at low is more likely to skip a search, stop early or skip a check, a poor trade for reading logs, where catching every failure is the point.



/models picks a model for the current session only; the config file is unchanged.
opencode run --model provider/model-id sets it for one run. The format is provider/model-id, with an optional #variant such as #high. IDs are case-sensitive.
The model key in opencode.json (or opencode.jsonc) sets your default.
An agent can have its own model key. A subagent with no model inherits the parent session’s model. The docs’ frontmatter example is mode: subagent plus model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5#high (sketch, not run).
A local Ollama model is selectable like any other, for example ollama/gemma3:4b, as the Adopt the Pet quest showed.

Not checked: which model OpenCode’s built-in general and explore subagents use, whether a small_model key exists, the file location for OpenCode agent files, and whether a local model is good enough as a cheap delegate (the docs only say it can be selected). Not checked: any way to run an Ollama model as a Claude Code subagent; Claude Code’s documented subagent model values are Claude aliases or Claude IDs only.

text:
Other model families and harnesses
Everything above uses Claude’s names and tiers. The ideas carry over to other families, and the names do not. Mistral is one example (docs read 2026-11-20 through a summarising tool; sources in research/mistral.md):

Models. Mistral’s overview page lists open-weight models (for example Ministral 3 in 3B, 8B and 14B, and Mistral Small 4, both Apache 2.0; Ollama’s mistral-small page may be an earlier release than Small 4) beside “Premier” models such as Codestral and its embedding and OCR models, which show no open licence. In the part of the models page we read, no Devstral model is listed as active. The hosted Devstral 2 was marked deprecated on 2026-05-22 and due to retire on 2026-07-31, a date that has passed. Check the page for current names.
Harness. Mistral Vibe is an open-source terminal coding agent (Apache 2.0). Its docs describe four approval modes: ask (asks before any tool), accept-edits (the default: file edits are applied without asking, shell commands still ask), smart-approve (a classifier; we did not read its details), and auto-approve (“Trusted, sandboxed environments only”). Project config loads only from folders you have trusted. It reads ~/.vibe/config.toml. General practice: start in ask until you trust the project.
Local models. The docs say Vibe supports any model served behind an OpenAI-compatible API and name vLLM, llama.cpp, LM Studio and Ollama. They give no Ollama recipe, so treat Ollama as untested.
Not run: Vibe itself. Not read directly: its instruction-file page (a search summary names AGENTS.md).

General practice: when you switch families, redo the worksheet in this quest. A tier ladder built on one vendor’s models does not transfer name for name.

title: Pick Your Companion
section: 4. When the output is not good enough: the upgrade ladder
text:
4. When the output is not good enough: the upgrade ladder
Climb one rung at a time and re-check after each.

Add a way to verify. A test, a script, a count against an independent tool, a second look that does not share the first one’s blind spot (the idea behind Ground Truth). Without it you cannot tell whether the next rungs helped.
Raise effort one level.
Change the model to the next tier up.

The order (check, then effort, then model) is one article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs, though the docs do say to give the agent something to verify against and that effort is often the better lever. The article is a claude.dev piece about choosing a Claude model (the page shows the byline Addy Osmani and the date 2026-11-09, but does not say who runs the site, so authorship is unverified; its numbers are not verified). I use only its ideas, in my own words.
The cheap-then-retry pattern is in Anthropic’s cost-and-intelligence guidance for the API (a docs page, “Optimizing for cost and intelligence”): if outcomes are checkable (tests, or a verifier, which is a separate check that tests the output), run at low effort and re-run only the failures at higher effort. Two caveats from the same page: a checker that passes bad work lets failures through, and a failure costs two runs of waiting time. The docs also say to compare cost per finished task, because failed tasks still cost money and a few hard tasks can carry much of the bill.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
5. Delegation hygiene

Keep the expensive model’s context lean. Sending bulk reading to a subagent keeps that reading out of the main conversation (documented benefit).
A subagent returns only a summary, and summaries omit and distort. Spot-check: ask for exact quotes or file paths and open two yourself (see Where Machines Fail). Many subagents returning long answers can also fill the main context again, per the docs.
State your rules in the delegation prompt. Per the docs, the built-in Explore and Plan subagents (Explore is a read-only search helper; Plan is a read-only research helper used in plan mode) skip CLAUDE.md (the instructions file the tool loads at session start; see Know Your Gear) for speed, so a rule like “never touch raw/” must be written into the task you hand them. Custom subagents load it unless set to skip it.
Keep edits on the main model. One article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs: let a cheaper subagent read and report, and make the changes on the model you trust most.
Switching model mid-conversation can change prompt-cache behaviour (the docs say so and may ask you to confirm). One article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs: compact first, or switch at a natural break; compacting means replacing the history with a short summary (see When to Start Fresh).
Change effort between sessions when you are comparing. The docs note that changing top-level effort mid-session also invalidates the cache.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
6. Measure on your own task
Pick one small real task that has an outcome check (a test that passes, a count that matches).

Choose two settings to compare, for example the same model at medium and high. Change only one thing.
For each, start a fresh session, run the task three times, and record pass or fail from the outcome check.
After each run, open /usage and note the “Usage by model” block. The dollar figure is an estimate computed locally at list price, and on a subscription you may see plan usage bars instead. /usage resets on /clear.
Compare cost per passing run. Three runs is a small sample: it can expose a big difference, and a small one needs more runs.

This is the same habit as the Forest quests Close the Loop (give the agent something to check against) and Test the Skill (compare behaviour with and without a change).

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
7. What you gave up
Choosing wrongly costs you in both directions. Too small or too low: the companion loses the thread, skips checks or stops early, and you redo the work, often after you have already trusted it. Too big or too high: the same job costs more and runs slower, and you may not notice because the answer looks fine. The checks above are how you notice either mistake.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
Exercise: assign six jobs
No model needed. For each mock job, write down a model (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus or Fable), an effort (low, medium, high) and whether you would use a subagent, then open the key.

Rename 200 sample IDs in a samplesheet to a new scheme, given a mapping table.
Summarise the methods section of one paper into five bullets for your lab notes.
Debug a Nextflow stage that fails on one sample and passes on the others.
Classify 5,000 free-text tissue labels into 12 categories, with 200 hand-labelled rows to check against.
Plan a refactor of a 600-line QC script that three other people depend on.
Explain an error message you have not seen before.



Answer key (General practice, not from the docs; several answers are defensible)


Probably no model at all. A mapping table and a script do this exactly, and a script cannot invent an ID. If you use a model, Haiku at low or medium, with a diff or count check; no subagent needed.
Sonnet, medium, no subagent. The text is short, so there is no context to protect. Check two claims against the paper yourself.
Sonnet at medium, raised to high or Opus if the first attempt fails and a test says so. Keep it in the main conversation, because the debugging needs the history. Add a failing test first (rung 1).
Haiku, a subagent or a batch script, medium. The 200 hand-labelled rows are your outcome check; re-run only the rows that disagree at a higher setting. Spot-check a sample of the rest.
Opus, high, in plan mode, main conversation. A weak plan is expensive downstream and other people depend on the script. Ask for a test plan too (see Plan Before You Edit).
Sonnet, low or medium, no subagent. It is a short, checkable question: try the suggested fix. Escalate when the explanation does not hold up.



Check what model and effort your tool is using right now (/model, /effort) and write them down.


Run the same small task at two settings and compare the result and /usage.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
Prerequisites: Recruit the Beast and The Locked Cabinet. Objective: say what a cloud session is, what leaves your machine when you start one, which jobs suit it and which stay local, and review what comes back. Time: about 15 minutes. The exercise is a worksheet on a mock file tree and needs no cloud account or model.
Last verified (docs, not run): research/claude-cloud.md sources on 2026-11-17; the claude-code-on-the-web, cloud-environments, permission-modes and data-usage pages were re-read live that day; plan terms, limits and retention periods change, check the docs
Some ideas below come from an article on claude.dev about Claude Code in the cloud (the page shows the byline Addy Osmani and the date 2026-10-06, but the page does not say who runs the site, so we have not verified who wrote it; its numbers are not verified). The explanations are in our own words, and we mark each idea that comes only from the article.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
The rule for this page






ImportantCloud sessions are for drafting scripts and documentation. Data analysis stays on your machine or the cluster.



Use a cloud session for writing scripts, updating documentation and similar low-risk text work. Real data, controlled data, sample sheets with identifiers, genotypes and results stay out of a cloud session and its repository. Analysis runs on your own machine or the cluster, under your data agreement.
Think of the cloud agent as a drafting helper that returns a branch (a named line of commits in git) which you review and then run yourself, where the data lives.


You can skip cloud sessions altogether; nothing on this site requires them. If you do use one, the rest of the page shows how to keep sensitive material at home.

title: Claude in the Cloud
Claude in the Cloud
text:
2. What leaves your machine
This is the part to read twice. When you start a cloud session:

Your repository contents are cloned onto Anthropic’s VM. Anthropic reads only the repository you start the session in.
Your prompts and everything the agent reads and writes go to the model.
The session transcript (the saved record of the whole conversation, including tool output) is stored by Anthropic so you can return to it later.
Retention (how long Anthropic keeps stored data) follows your account type. The docs say: consumer plans keep it 5 years if you allow training and 30 days if you do not; commercial plans (Team, Enterprise, API) keep it 30 days as standard. These figures are time-sensitive. Check your own plan and the current docs. Deleting a cloud session permanently removes its event data.
All outbound traffic from Anthropic-hosted sessions passes through a proxy (a go-between server that forwards requests, here for audit logging and abuse prevention).
Network level None may still let data exit. A network access level is the setting that says which internet hosts the VM may reach (None, Limited or Full; see section 5). The docs say the Anthropic API stays reachable even at None, “which may allow data to exit the VM”.
Environment variables (named settings handed to programs, often used for keys) set in a cloud environment can be read by any command Claude runs, and the docs say anyone who uses that environment can read the values.
Sharing: a session can be visible to others. The docs warn sessions may contain code and credentials from private repositories.

Three organisation settings block cloud sessions outright, per the docs: compliance configurations, namely Zero Data Retention, a HIPAA configuration (HIPAA is the US health-data privacy law) and customer-managed encryption keys (your organisation holds the keys). If your organisation uses one of them, cloud sessions are not available. Your administrator can also switch cloud sessions off (the allow_remote_sessions policy).
This site’s rule (our own rule; the docs make no such claim): keep controlled data out of the cloud repository. The docs read for this page give no guidance for genomic, patient or other controlled-access data, and no statement on where cloud-session data is stored. Treat the clone, the transcript and anything you paste as held by Anthropic. The guidance on data agreements is in The Locked Cabinet; read it before you push anything to a remote that a cloud session can see (a remote is the copy of a repository hosted elsewhere, such as on GitHub).

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
3. Good uses and bad uses







Fine for a cloud session (code and mock data only)
Keep for your machine or the cluster




Write a samplesheet validator, tested on a three-row mock file
Run the analysis


Write a QC summary plotting script, developed on mock data
Load real counts, genotypes or results


Draft or update the README, changelog, docstrings
Debug with real sample IDs in the repository


Refactor non-data code that has tests
Anything under a data agreement


Review a pull request (read the diff, suggest changes), if it holds no identifiers
Anything that needs a local database or the cluster


Triage issues (sort, label, summarise), if they hold no identifiers
Anything that needs your institution’s network or files



The last two rows on the right are partly our inference: the docs do not mention VPN, on-prem network access or mounting local or cluster filesystems, and list a roughly 30 GB disk, so assume none of that is there. One article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs: local work beats the cloud when you need local databases, a VPN or special hardware.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
4. How to start

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Push first. claude --cloud "your task" starts a cloud session from your terminal, and it clones the GitHub remote at your current branch (your local folder is not used). Commit and push (save snapshots, then upload them to the remote) before you start, so the session sees your latest work. If the branch is not on GitHub the CLI says Branch <name> is not on GitHub, and the session starts from a pushed commit or the default branch. One repository per session. You can also start from claude.ai/code in the browser.
Write a ticket-style prompt, that is, a self-contained note like a work ticket: the problem, the expected result, and a command that proves it (in the example, pytest, a Python test runner). The docs say to be specific, name files and paste errors. The proof-command habit is one article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs. Example, with no data in it:
Problem: scripts/validate_samplesheet.py accepts duplicate sample IDs.
Expected: exit status 1 and a message naming the duplicated ID.
Check: pytest tests/test_validate_samplesheet.py (mock rows only).
Add a test for the duplicate case. Only change files under scripts/ and tests/.
This repository has no data/ or results/ folders, and that is deliberate: a prompt line such as “do not read data/” is a request to the model and gives no protection. If the folder is in the repository, the cloud session can read it.
If there is no remote. When a repository has no GitHub remote, or the Claude GitHub App (a program you install on a repository or organisation to grant it limited access) is not on it, Claude Code instead bundles the repository and uploads it: full history of all branches plus uncommitted changes to tracked files, under 100 MB. Untracked files are left out. On macOS, Linux and WSL the upload also needs git 2.31 or later; with an older git the CLI refuses to start the session and tells you to update. On those systems, uncommitted changes to .env, *.pem, *.tfvars, id_rsa and Git LFS-managed files (large files stored outside normal git history) are skipped (on native Windows everything tracked uploads). Keep data out of this route entirely. Your history may already hold a file you deleted, and the bundle takes all of it. Check what is tracked and what your .gitignore covers before you go anywhere near this. Non-GitHub hosts can only use the bundle, and cannot push back.
/web-setup, typed inside Claude Code (not in your shell), sends your gh auth token (GitHub’s command-line login token) to Anthropic so cloud sessions can reach your repositories without the GitHub App. It needs a claude.ai sign-in; API-key sign-in does not work, and neither does a Bedrock or Vertex-style provider. On Team and Enterprise plans an Owner has to enable it first.
Getting the session back: teleport. To teleport is to pull a cloud session into your local terminal: claude --teleport (shows a picker), claude --teleport <session-id>, or /teleport (alias /tp, a shorter name for the same command) inside a session. It needs a clean git state (it offers to stash your changes, that is, set them aside temporarily with git stash), the same repository (not a fork, which is your own copy of someone else’s repository), the branch pushed, and the same claude.ai account.
GitHub access, in short. Two ways in: the GitHub App or your /web-setup token. For Anthropic-hosted sessions, your GitHub credential is stored encrypted on Anthropic’s servers and does not enter the VM; the VM holds a short-lived credential, and a GitHub proxy swaps it in. The proxy rejects branch deletions and tag pushes, but it does not limit which branches a push can update. To limit that, use GitHub branch protection or rulesets (rules on which branches may be changed and by whom); the docs note a rule that the connected access can bypass will not block the push. The docs do not describe a credential limited to one branch, so plan without one.


We found no hosted cloud-session feature for OpenCode. Its docs describe opencode pair (a web interface opened through a one-time local link), Docker images, and its own model-access services, which are not hosted agent sessions. Not checked: whether Ollama has any such feature. So there is no equivalent to teach here. The closest thing is to run OpenCode yourself in your own container or virtual machine, which is your own infrastructure and your own responsibility.
As The Locked Cabinet says, a local Ollama model keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls the agent makes may not. If your data agreement rules out third-party processing, that local route is the one to ask about.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
5. Environments
An environment is a saved configuration for cloud sessions: network access, environment variables, a setup script and network secrets. A first-time setup creates one called Default, with Limited access.
Network access levels, using the docs’ current names:







Level
What the VM can reach




None
No internet (the Anthropic API, the GitHub proxy and enabled connectors still work)


Limited
A default allowlist (a list of the only hosts permitted) of package registries, GitHub and cloud SDKs, plus domains you add


Full
Any host



One article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs: pick the narrowest level that lets the task finish. The docs show the levels and give no recommendation.
Setup scripts. A setup script is a Bash script that runs once as root before Claude starts, to install what the task needs. It must exit with status 0, and the docs say keep it under about five minutes or it is not cached. The result is cached as a filesystem snapshot (packages and files stay; running processes and databases do not), and rebuilt when the script or allowed hosts change or after about 7 days. Installs need network access, so None blocks them.
Environment variables versus network secrets. Environment variables are readable (see section 2). Network secrets are the docs’ safer option where possible: the key stays outside the VM, and Anthropic’s agent proxy adds it to requests to hosts you list.
Preinstalled tools. The docs list Python with pip, uv, poetry and pytest, Node, Ruby, PHP, Java, Go, Rust, C and C++, Docker, PostgreSQL 16, Redis, git, gh and jq. No R, conda or bioinformatics tools are listed. This describes what the VM contains; analysis stays local. Ask Claude to run check-tools to see what is actually present.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
6. Permission modes in the cloud
A permission mode says how much the agent may do before asking you (see Grow the Carapace). Cloud sessions offer three: Accept edits, Plan and Auto (Auto can be switched off by your organisation). There is no Manual and no Bypass mode in the cloud, and a bypassPermissions setting in your files is ignored there. You pick the mode in the dropdown; there is no --cloud flag for it.
Use Plan for anything you do not already understand, and read the plan before it edits: see Plan Before You Edit. The docs also describe planning locally with claude --permission-mode plan, committing and pushing the plan, and then starting claude --cloud.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
7. Limits and failure modes

A fresh machine every time. The docs say an idle VM pauses and may later be reclaimed (taken back by the system). Files are kept while it is paused; plan on them being gone afterwards (our inference). Reopening restores the conversation, but running commands and subagents (helper agents the main agent started) are lost. One article’s habit, not confirmed in the docs: commit as you go, so work is not lost if the machine is reclaimed.
Timeouts. A foreground command defaults to 2 minutes (up to 10), then moves to the background for up to 30 more.
Size. The docs give approximate ceilings of 4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM and 30 GB disk, and say heavy jobs may be stopped.
Shared usage. Cloud work counts against the same plan limits as all your other Claude Code use (time-sensitive: check your plan). One article’s claim, not confirmed in the docs: several parallel sessions use the limit proportionately faster.
No local services. No GPU, VPN or cluster access is documented (inference, see section 3).
GitHub comments under your name. Claude can reply on pull requests under your GitHub name, labelled as Claude Code. That can trigger any comment-driven automation you have set up.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
8. Review what comes back
The result is a branch. Treat it like a stranger’s pull request: it may be fine and it may be wrong.

Read the diff (the list of changed lines) as you would any other. The habits are in The Wall of Output and The Reviewer’s Code.
Look for accidents in the diff: committed data files, absolute paths, sample IDs in a test or a comment, a .env, a notebook saved with outputs (a notebook is a Jupyter document mixing code and results; its saved outputs are the tables and plots stored inside the file).
Run the tests locally, on your machine.
Only then run the script on your data, locally or on the cluster, under your data agreement. The cloud agent never saw that data and never ran that step.

A green test in the cloud is a claim to verify. A test passing on mock data tells you the script runs; your real data is the next check, run locally.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
Exercise: the safe-to-send checklist
No cloud account and no model needed. Open tree.txt, a mock repository tree (every name is invented).

Mark each path that must not reach anything a cloud session can see. Say whether it needs removing from history (it is already committed) or only ignoring, and write one reason each.
Write the .gitignore lines that would have stopped it.
Draft a ticket-style prompt for one low-risk task: update docs/usage.md, or add a missing-column test to scripts/validate_samplesheet.py. Include the problem, the expected result and a check that uses only data/mock/.



Answer key (our judgement; some entries depend on your data agreement)

Every listed path below is in the tree as committed, so each one needs removing from history before you push anything a cloud session can see. The ignore lines further down only prevent a repeat.
Paths to remove:

.env: a secret. It was already committed, so remove it from history and replace the token; ignoring it helps only from now on.
samplesheet_real.csv: identifiers and genotype calls.
data/raw/ and data/processed/: real reads and real counts.
notebooks/01_qc.ipynb and notebooks/02_diffexp.ipynb: outputs saved inside them contain real sample IDs, tables and plots. Clear the outputs, or keep the notebooks out.
results/ (including de_genes.csv and pca_real_samples.png): results.
logs/slurm-482913.out: real sample IDs and cluster paths.
notebooks/.ipynb_checkpoints/: autosave copies of the notebooks, with the same saved outputs.

Fine to send (they hold no real data): README.md, environment.yml, samplesheet_template.csv, config/params.yaml (check it for real paths), data/mock/, docs/, scripts/, tests/.
Ignore lines that would help (general practice, not from the docs):
.env
.env.*
samplesheet_real.csv
*.fastq.gz
data/raw/
data/processed/
results/
logs/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
General practice, not a vendor claim: add a rule for notebooks too (for example, a pre-commit hook, a script git runs automatically before each commit, that clears outputs), because .gitignore alone cannot strip outputs from a notebook you do want to commit. Likewise, .gitignore only stops files that are not yet tracked; anything already committed stays in history until you remove it properly, and rewriting history is its own careful job (see Save Point).
Sample prompt:
Problem: docs/usage.md does not mention the --strandedness option added in v0.3.
Expected: a short section with the option, its allowed values, and one example
command using data/mock/ only.
Check: the example command in the new section runs on data/mock/counts_mock.tsv. Only edit docs/usage.md.
Remember that a prompt line is a request. The safe version of this repository has no real data folders to read.


Look up your data agreement and check whether it allows any third-party processing before you ever push to a cloud-connected remote.


Check whether your organisation’s plan allows cloud sessions at all.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
What to remember

Cloud sessions are for drafting scripts and documentation; analysis stays on your machine or the cluster. Real data, controlled data, sample sheets with identifiers, genotypes and results stay out of a cloud session and its repository.
Your repository contents, prompts and session transcript go to Anthropic, and network level None may still let data exit the VM.
Return is a branch: read the diff, look for stray data, run the tests locally, then run on your data where it lives, under your data agreement.

title: Plug In a Server
text:
Prerequisites: Grow the Carapace (permission rules). Walk the trunk first. Objective: treat an MCP server as software you install, then scope it, limit it and read what it sends back. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code docs and OpenCode V2 docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/tools-and-guards.md and research/terminology.md)
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is, in its own words, “an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems”. A server is the piece on the other side: it offers the harness tools or data, such as an issue tracker, a database or a monitoring system. MCP is optional. It widens what the agent can reach, and every widening is a decision.

title: Plug In a Server
section: A server is software you installed
text:
A server is software you installed
A stdio server (a program the harness starts locally and talks to over its input/output) is a command that Claude Code launches on your machine (claude mcp add ... -- <command>), and secrets can be passed to it as environment variables. So a reasonable working assumption, offered as general practice (our wording, outside the docs), is that it can do whatever that command can do with the credentials you gave it. The docs’ one security sentence is short: “Verify you trust each server before connecting it. Servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection risk.” (Prompt injection: text from a file, web page or tool that the model treats as an instruction.)

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Adding a remote server over HTTP (the transport: how the harness talks to the server; an http server is remote), and a local one (everything after -- is passed to the server untouched):
claude mcp add --transport http mydocs https://example.com/mcp
claude mcp add --env API_KEY=your-key-here myserver -- <command> [args...]
The --env line is an unrun sketch of the syntax; check claude mcp add --help for the current flags. Inside a session, /mcp lists the servers and their tools. An older transport called SSE (server-sent events, one-way streaming over HTTP) is deprecated in favour of HTTP where a server offers both.
Three scopes (scope = who or where a setting applies) decide who gets the server (set with -s/--scope):







Scope
Where it applies




Local (the default)
this project only, for you alone; stored in ~/.claude.json


Project
everyone on the project, via .mcp.json in the project root


User
all your projects; stored in ~/.claude.json



A project-scoped server is a file in the repository:
{ "mcpServers": { "shared-server": { "type": "http", "url": "https://example.com/mcp" } } }
For security reasons, Claude Code asks for approval in interactive sessions before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json. claude mcp reset-project-choices resets your answers. Read that file as you would read a script from a stranger’s repository, because it asks to start something on your machine. In claude -p and Agent SDK (software development kit) runs, which are headless (non-interactive), there is no prompt: the docs say project-scoped servers load without asking, and name --strict-mcp-config among the mitigations.
Each server’s tools appear in permission rules as mcp__<server>__<tool>, and mcp__<server>__* (a matcher, a pattern that selects names) matches every tool of one server. Tool definitions are deferred (loaded only when needed) by default, so only tool names and server instructions take up context until a tool is used.


In the V2 docs, servers go under mcp.servers, and V2 does not put server names directly under mcp (check which version you have installed). A remote server:
{ "mcp": { "servers": { "mydocs": {
    "type": "remote",
    "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:MCP_API_KEY}" } } } } }
A local one uses "type": "local" and a command array. Set "disabled": true to switch a server off. The docs say that “MCP tools consume model context, so add only the servers you need.”
Permissions are an ordered array where the last match wins and no match means ask. An MCP tool’s action is <server>_<tool> with resource *. Not checked: project-level approval prompts for OpenCode servers, and how a local Ollama model changes any of this. Check the current docs.

title: Plug In a Server
section: What comes back is text to read
text:
What comes back is text to read
A server that fetches web pages, tickets or messages hands text written by someone else to the model. Prompt injection means that text can contain sentences aimed at the agent (“ignore the above and …”) and the model may follow them. The docs give one sentence on this, so the rest is general practice:

Prefer read-only servers and read-only credentials. A server that cannot write cannot be talked into writing.
Give it the least privilege (only the access the job needs) that does the job: one project, one scope, a token limited to what you need.
Read before adding: who publishes it, what tools it lists, what it asks for. Unneeded servers are also unneeded context.
Read fetched content sceptically, and supervise any write access an agent uses on it.
Permission rules still apply to server tools, so deny the dangerous ones by name.

The AI for Science best practices (a European draft with no endorsements yet; practice 3) add a habit for the where from question. Servers, skills and plugins either run code or supply instructions to the agent, so each is a way in. A listing in a registry says the thing is easy to find and says nothing about a security review; the page notes that the official MCP registry lists self-reported data and runs no security review. Prefer a source that records the maintainer and a review date, and check what the interface is allowed to do. If your institution has no vetted list, treat every interface as unvetted; asking for such a list is our own suggestion (General practice). Their examples include a server whose tool description carried hidden instructions, and a skill whose instructions told the agent to post results to an outside endpoint. Not checked first-hand: read 2026-11-20 through a fetch summary, so re-check the wording on the page; see research/aiforscience.md.






Note



Claude Code’s docs also say that sandbox restrictions still apply even if a prompt injection bypasses the model’s decision-making. The sandbox covers shell commands, and a server might take other routes, so treat it as one layer.



Pick an MCP server you might use. Write down who publishes it, the tools it lists, the credential it needs, and whether a read-only version exists. Hold off installing it for now.

title: Advice or Enforcement
text:
Prerequisites: Guard the Door. Objective: sort every control on this site by whether it advises, asks or enforces, and choose the right one for each risk. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code docs and OpenCode V2 docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/tools-and-guards.md)
Every control you have met does one of three things.
The Gatehouse’s rule of thumb: advice for preferences, a prompt for decisions you want to make each time, enforcement for things that must never happen.

title: Advice or Enforcement
text:
Each control, and its edge

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama










Control
Kind
Edge, per the docs read or earlier quests




CLAUDE.md, Skill text, your prompt
Advises
Influences the model only.


Permission prompt or ask rule
Asks
You must read it. A project .mcp.json server has its own approval prompt, and -p runs (non-interactive, headless) cannot show it.


deny rule
Enforces
Matching on command arguments is fragile (see the Carapace quest). Deny and ask rules are still evaluated when a hook returns allow.


PreToolUse hook, exit 2
Enforces
Fires only on tool calls, sees the literal text, fails open if it crashes.


Sandbox
Enforces
Off by default, and limits shell commands only (see the Carapace quest). The docs say its restrictions still apply if a prompt injection bypasses the model’s decision.


Git history
Recovers
Recovery only, with no prevention: a commit is a restore point that exists whatever the model did next.



A hook that exits 0 with no JSON decision adds no control: it expresses no decision and the normal permission flow runs. (A hook can also exit 0 and print a JSON deny decision, which does block.)










Control
Kind
Edge, per the V2 docs read




Instructions file, Skill text, your prompt
Advises
Influences the model only.


Permission rule with effect ask; no matching rule
Asks
No match means ask.


Permission rule with effect deny
Enforces
An explicit configured deny is final and does not invoke the hook.


Plugin permission hook (evaluate)
Enforces when it denies
Runs for allow and ask decisions, and can change the effect to deny.


Git history
Recovers
Recovery only; it prevents nothing.



Not checked for OpenCode: an exit-code-2 equivalent, whether throwing in a tool hook blocks a call, sandboxing, and the effect of a local Ollama model. Check the current docs before counting on any of them.

section: Choose by the cost of being wrong
text:
Choose by the cost of being wrong








Risk
Control
Why




Style: prefer snake_case, tidy commit messages
Advice
A miss costs a review comment.


Pushing to a shared branch
Ask
You want to decide each time, with context.


Reading .env or key files
Deny rule on the Read tool, plus sandbox or hook for Bash (enforce); still not total
It must never happen, so use enforcement, and cover each route the agent could use.


A specific destructive command you can name
Blocking hook (enforce)
Code refuses it. It covers only what it matches.


Fetched text telling the agent to act
Least privilege, read-only servers, sceptical reading
Advice may not hold against text the model has already read, so limit what the agent can do.


An experiment that might wreck your files
Git commit plus a scratch folder
Recovery only; it prevents nothing.



Layer them: advice to steer, enforcement for the non-negotiable, git for the day something slips through. None of them replaces reading the diff.
The AI for Science best practices (a European draft with no endorsements yet) make the same split for research groups and add a few habits. Put limits in the system that runs the agent: permission scopes, and spend caps in the metering system (the system that counts usage and cost), because a budget the agent can exceed is not a limit. Give each agent duty a named human owner. Log what an agent did under an identity you can trace. Institutions are advised to keep a list of the agents in use, including personal ones connected to mail or files; a group can keep its own (General practice). Their example is an over-privileged agent with shell access that wiped data on a shared lab server. The page advises a scoped account, a backup before write or delete access, and a named owner for the machine. Not checked first-hand: the practice page, read 2026-11-20 through a fetch summary, so re-check the wording on the page; see research/aiforscience.md.

text: Prerequisites: Write the Brief. Objective: ask an agent for a plan before it edits, review that plan like a reviewer, and know what a plan guarantees and where its limits lie. Time: about 20 minutes. Nothing here runs a model; the exercise uses mock files on your laptop. Last verified (docs, not run): research/plan-mode.md sources on 2026-11-16. Claude Code details come from the official docs; the OpenCode part is deliberately short. Items marked General practice or Not checked are not from the docs. title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Why plan first
A wrong plan costs you a paragraph to read and reject. A wrong 400-line diff (the list of lines a change added and removed) costs you the time to review it, and, General practice, the longer it is, the more likely you approve something you did not understand. Later in the Maze, the Wall of Output makes the same point: only accept as much output as you can honestly review, and ask for smaller pieces. A plan is the cheapest piece to ask for first.
The Claude Code docs say to use plan mode “for changes you want to review before they touch disk”. That is the only official when-to-plan line we found; the rest of this page says which parts are docs and which are habits.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
How: plan mode
Words used below. A session is one conversation with the agent. Shell commands are commands you would type in a terminal, such as ls or git status. Context is everything the model can see in the session. A subagent is a helper with its own context window; only its summary comes back. A deny rule is a rule that blocks an action, and it applies in every mode. Auto mode is a mode where a background check decides what runs without a prompt. Bypass permissions is a startup option (--dangerously-skip-permissions) that turns most prompts off. -p runs one command with no chat (non-interactive mode). The Agent SDK is a library for building your own agent programs.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Plan mode is a permission mode: a setting for what the agent may do without asking you. (The Kennel quest Recruit the Beast introduced the modes and the first run; this page does not repeat it.) In plan mode the agent reads files, may run shell commands to explore, and writes a plan, and is meant to leave your source files unedited until you approve the plan (tell it to go ahead; not always enforced, see the limits below).
Three ways in:

Shift+Tab during a session, until the status bar shows ⏸ plan mode on.
/plan followed by your request, for example /plan add a strandedness column to the samplesheet parser.
claude --permission-mode plan when you start it.

When the plan is ready, the agent presents it and asks how to proceed. The options, with their exact labels:

Yes, and use auto mode. Auto mode decides what runs without a prompt. If auto mode is unavailable, this reads Yes, auto-accept edits. If your session started with bypass, it reads Yes, and switch to BYPASS PERMISSIONS (no further prompts) for this session. Bypass skips most prompts.
Yes, manually approve edits. Each edit still asks you.
No, keep planning. You say what to change.

A setting, showClearContextOnPlanAccept, adds a first option that approves and also clears the planning context . The docs page does not give its label, and we did not confirm whether it is on or off by default.






Warning



The trap. At the approval prompt, Shift+Tab approves the plan. If you want to think, change something or back out, press Esc first. To leave plan mode when no prompt is open, press Shift+Tab.


Where the plan lives. Plans are written to ~/.claude/plans/ by default (the plansDirectory setting changes the folder). Ctrl+G opens the proposed plan in your default text editor so you can edit it before the agent proceeds. Approving exits plan mode and switches to the mode you chose; to plan again, use Shift+Tab or /plan.
Side helper. In plan mode the agent can hand research to the built-in Plan subagent. It is read-only, so the main conversation stays read-only too.


OpenCode has a built-in plan agent. Per the docs it explores and plans without editing normal project files, and it can edit only under its plan directory, ~/.opencode/plan. That edit restriction is a deny rule, and saved approvals do not override a deny. Its shell commands stay under the normal permission rules. The base policy for every agent is allow everything except asking before reading .env files, so shell commands are likely to run without a prompt: confirm in your version.
You can turn the plan agent off with {"agents": {"plan": {"disabled": true}}}.
Not checked: how to switch to the plan agent in your version (we found no documented key or /plan command), whether there is any plan approval step, and the rest of its default rules. Its approval flow may differ from Claude Code’s prompt, so the OpenCode agents page is the place to check.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: Review the plan like a reviewer
text:
Review the plan like a reviewer
A plan is text from a model that has not yet run anything. Read it the way you would read a methods section from a collaborator you have not worked with before. General practice (not from the docs), a checklist:

What files will it touch? Anything outside the task is a question to ask.
What does it assume about the data? “IDs are unique” or “the file has a header” are guesses until checked against the real files.
What could it break? Callers, config, tests, outputs other people read.
How will it verify, and is the check independent of the code it writes? A test the agent writes for its own code can share its mistake. Compute one value some other way, as in the Ground Truth quest later in the Maze.
Are the steps small enough to review one at a time? A step names one change, so “Update everything” needs splitting.
What is not in the plan? Missing edge cases, missing tests, no mention of a rollback.

If an answer is bad, choose No, keep planning and say what to change, or edit the plan yourself with Ctrl+G.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: What a plan does not guarantee
text:
What a plan does not guarantee

A plan is advice. General practice: an approved plan is only as good as your review of it.
The agent can deviate. General practice: the agent can still change course after approval. Afterwards, read the diff against the plan: every changed file should be one the plan named. The docs also describe /code-review, which reviews the diff in a fresh subagent that never saw your conversation.
Plan mode may not be enforced. In an interactive terminal session where bypass permissions is available, the docs say Claude is only instructed to plan without editing. Claude Code does not enforce it, and edits and shell commands run without a prompt (explicit ask rules and a few critical deletions still prompt). With -p (non-interactive mode), the Agent SDK and the VS Code chat panel, the blocks stay in place.
Deny rules always apply. A deny rule is a rule that blocks an action. It blocks in every mode, plan mode included.
“Read-only” has limits. Not checked: how MCP tools behave in plan mode, and whether a read-only shell command can have side effects. Do not read “plan mode” as “nothing can happen”.
It lives outside your repository by default. The plan file sits in ~/.claude/plans/. Not checked: whether /rewind covers it. Keep your own project under Git.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: When to plan, and when not to
text:
When to plan, and when not to
From the docs: use plan mode for changes you want to review before they touch disk, and a vague prompt is fine when exploring, at the cost of more correction. The first two bullets below are General practice:

A one-line fix with an obvious check: just ask for it.
Unfamiliar code, changes across several files, and anything that touches paths where your data lives: plan first.
Open-ended exploring: a vague prompt is fine (docs, above).

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Keep the approved plan
The plan in ~/.claude/plans/ is easy to lose track of. General practice: ask the agent to save the approved plan into your project, for example as PLAN.md, then commit it. The docs describe a related pattern: ask the agent to interview you until it could write the spec, save it as SPEC.md, then start a fresh session (an empty conversation) to build from it. The fresh session has a clean context and a written definition of done. The Codon Mill quest Handoff Notes covers what such a file should hold.

title: Plan Before You Edit

Exercise: review a bad plan
Everything here is a mock on your laptop. Nothing is run through a model. Save mock-plan.md and samplesheet.csv. The plan says it will make a samplesheet parser accept a new strandedness column. Read the CSV, then go through the six checklist questions and write down every problem you find. Aim for at least four.


Answer key


No verification step. Step 6 reports success, and no step runs the parser or compares against an independent count.
A file outside the parser. Step 4 edits conf/base.config and renames a parameter, which can break every command line and config that uses the old name. The task covered only the parser.
An unchecked assumption about the data. Step 3 says sample IDs are unique. In the CSV, S03 appears twice (lanes L1 and L2), so a dictionary keyed by sample_id silently keeps only one row.
One step is too big. Step 5 covers modules, docs and tests at once. Ask for it to be split and reviewed piece by piece.
Also worth noting: S04 has an empty fastq_2, and the plan leaves that open (what is not in the plan). Step 2’s default of unstranded may quietly hide a missing column in a real run.



Review the plan the agent proposes for your next real task with the checklist before approving. Write down one thing you changed or rejected.

title: Close the Loop
text:
Prerequisites: Forge a Skill. Objective: turn “it did the wrong thing” into a measured fix, and know when the fix has stopped working. Time: about 10 minutes. General practice.
Sooner or later the agent does something you did not want: it skips a check, names files badly, or uses a method your lab avoids. A chat correction helps that one reply, and a Skill helps next time. An eval tells you whether the fix works, and keeps telling you after the model or tool changes.

title: Close the Loop
text:
What is an eval?
An eval (short for evaluation) is a repeatable check of how well an AI system does a task. It is the AI version of a unit test, with one difference. Ordinary code gives the same output for the same input, so a test can assert one answer. A model can answer the same prompt differently each time, so you run the check several times and ask how often, and how well, it does the job.
Trying a few favourite prompts and judging whether it “feels better” is a quick start but a weak habit. A new model, a new prompt or a new Skill can help one task and hurt another, and you will not see it from a handful of tries. An eval runs the same cases every time, so a change shows up as a number you can compare.
An eval has three parts:

Cases: the prompts you test with, plus what a good answer looks like.
Task: the thing under test, here the agent with or without your Skill.
Graders: the checks that mark each answer.

Graders come in three kinds:









Kind
How it marks
Strength
Weakness




Deterministic
A script checks something exact: the file exists, the command ran, the output has 3 columns.
Free, fast, same result every time.
Covers only what you can state as a rule.


Human
You read the output and judge it.
Best for quality, style and “is this actually right?”.
Slow and does not scale. Often the only option at the start.


Judge model
A second model marks the answer against a rubric.
Handles open-ended output at scale.
Costs a model call per mark, and the judge can be wrong.



Use deterministic graders wherever you can, a person where you must, and a judge model for the rest. Because answers vary, the result is usually a pass rate (for example 2 of 3 runs, or 80% of graders passed) and not one pass or fail. The useful question is whether a change moved that number up or down.






Note



Cases decide how good the eval is. A set of cases should look like your real work and include awkward ones: an empty file, a misspelt name, a request phrased differently. Ten realistic cases beat a hundred invented ones. Real failures are the best source, which is why the loop below starts with Notice.

title: Close the Loop
text:
The loop

Notice. Something did not go your way. Write down the prompt you used and what was wrong with the result.
Steer. Write or edit a Skill (or an instructions-file line) that says what to do instead. Keep it short and concrete.
Measure. Run the same prompt with the Skill and without it, several times each. Models vary between runs, so several tries give a fairer picture than one.
Compare. If with is clearly better than without, the Skill earns its place. If they are about the same, the Skill adds little: it may not be triggering, it may repeat what the model already does, or it may be too vague.
Repeat later. A new model version can make a Skill unnecessary, or break it. Re-run the evals when the model, the tool, or the Skill changes.







Note



The unit that matters is the difference between with and without. The without run is the baseline: the run without the change, which tells you what the model does on its own. A Skill that scores 100% both ways has added nothing the model lacked.

title: Close the Loop
text:
What to check

The result: does the output have what you asked for (a file exists, a command was run, a number matches)? Prefer checks a script can do.
The process: was the Skill actually used? A good-looking answer without the Skill loading means the Skill is not the reason.
Cost: every run is a real model call. Start with few cases and few runs, and raise them only for a Skill you will rely on.

Evals can be wrong too. A check that always passes, or that fails correct answers, tells you little. Read a few raw outputs by hand before trusting a score.
The AI for Science best practices (a European draft with no endorsements yet; practice 8) add four habits for judging a tool before you rely on it. Test on cases with known answers. Repeat the runs, since one pass can be luck. Write down the failure modes you see. Test again when the tool, the model or your task changes. They also say a judge model from the same family as the one being judged is not an independent grader, and that when a model does grade, you should check a sample by hand against reference answers fixed in advance. Not checked first-hand: read 2026-11-20 through a fetch summary, so re-check the wording on the page; see research/aiforscience.md.

Keep a short list of the times an agent went wrong for you. Each entry is a candidate Skill and a ready-made eval case.

title: The Locked Cabinet
text:
Prerequisites: Grow the Carapace. Objective: keep keys, settings and sensitive data out of the agent’s reach, and know what changes on a shared cluster. Time: about 15 minutes. Much research data is not sensitive. Some of it is, and then special agreements apply. This quest uses no real data and practises habits, so that the careful choice becomes automatic.

title: The Locked Cabinet
text:
Three ideas

A prompt may leave your machine. With a hosted model, anything the agent reads may be sent to the provider. A model running locally (the Pet, via Ollama) keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls it makes may not. Whether either is allowed for your data is decided by your agreement.
Secrets stay out of content. API keys, tokens, SSH keys and passwords belong in a secret store, kept out of the project folder, and out of chats and any instructions file you commit. Be aware that an environment variable is visible to any command the agent runs, so a read rule alone is not a seal.
A shared cluster is shared. What is fine on your laptop can disturb other people on a login node, or break a data policy on shared storage. Cluster rules apply to agents exactly as they apply to you.







Note



A deny rule on your secrets files (see Grow the Carapace) stops the agent’s file-reading tool. An agent that can run shell commands may still be able to read them another way, so also keep secrets out of the project folder, and use a sandbox or shell rules where you can. Not confirmed here: exactly how each tool treats shell reads of denied files.



What the European draft best practices add
The AI for Science best practices (a draft with no endorsements yet; practice 11) say the same about sending data and add three points. Not checked first-hand: read 2026-11-20 through a fetch summary, so re-check the wording on the page; see research/aiforscience.md.

Reading a file already discloses it. With an externally hosted model, everything the agent reads goes to the provider. Their example is an agent that opens a project .env file: the keys now sit in the provider’s logs under your account’s retention terms, so rotate them, and keep secrets outside folders the agent can read.
Personal data needs more than a no-training promise. Sending personal data to a provider is processing under GDPR (the EU data protection law). That needs a lawful basis (a legal reason to process), a processor contract (a written agreement with the provider) and, outside the EU, a transfer basis (a legal route for sending data abroad), even when the provider does not train on it. Ask your data steward which accounts are approved (General practice), and use an institutional account for work.
Limit where the agent can send data through its environment. Instructions alone do not stop a send. A sandbox or network limit can.

title: The Locked Cabinet
text:
What stays behind: transcripts
The agent keeps a record of the session so that it can resume. Anything that passes through a tool goes into that record: file contents, command output, pasted text. Claude Code’s docs say that if a tool reads a .env file or a command prints a credential, the value is written to the session transcript, stored locally in plaintext (for 30 days by default). Read 2026-11-23 on the docs pages listed in research/transcripts-and-secrets.md; no command was run.
A real case: in November 2026 a coding-tool vendor published an account of an incident in which a bucket of agent traces, shared with a vendor for training, was copied. It said a small number of traces held credentials that had not been redacted. We read the vendor’s own post; the numbers are theirs.
Habits that cost little:

Reference a secret, do not type it. Write psql "$DATABASE_URL", so the command, and any rule saved from it, holds a variable’s name. When you choose “Yes, and don’t ask again”, Claude Code saves a rule in .claude/settings.local.json, which it keeps out of git through your global excludes only. Reported by users, not confirmed in the docs: a password typed into an approved command can end up in that file.
Approve patterns, not literal commands (npm run *).
Rotate anything that has been in a transcript. Deleting the file does not reach backups, copies or a vendor’s storage.
Keep less. cleanupPeriodDays shortens how long transcripts stay, claude purge deletes a project’s state (try --dry-run first), and CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY=1 skips writing them.
Make a leak worth little (General practice). A token for one repository that expires in an hour is a small loss if it leaks. GitHub says an installation access token expires after 1 hour. Where a service only issues long-lived keys, give the agent a separate, narrow key that you can rotate without breaking your own work.

Redaction helps and has limits. A scanner matches formats, and a password after -p has none. The docs also say deny rules on files do not stop a script the agent runs from reading them.

title: The Locked Cabinet
text:
Unpublished ideas and results
A common worry: my unpublished results or ideas will leak and someone will get there first. Another version is a company showing a proof of something you spent years on. This page does not claim either has happened. The habits below lower the chance and the cost of being wrong.
What the docs say (Claude Code data usage page, read 2026-11-17):

Training use means a provider may learn from your prompts to improve future models. For Free, Pro, Max and Ultra accounts it depends on a privacy setting that you can change. For Team, Enterprise and API accounts, Anthropic says it does not train on code or prompts sent to Claude Code under commercial terms, unless the customer opts in.
Retention for consumer accounts is 5 years if you allow model improvement and 30 days if you do not. Commercial accounts have 30 days as standard, and zero data retention for qualified Enterprise accounts.
Not checked: the claude.ai chat privacy pages and the full terms. Read the terms of the exact tool and plan you use.

For comparison, Mistral’s help and docs pages (read 2026-11-20 through a summarising tool, so re-check the wording before you rely on it; sources in research/mistral.md):

Training use depends on the product and plan. Mistral’s help pages say that Vibe users are not opted out by default (Vibe Free, Pro, Teams and Student have training on with an opt-out; Vibe Enterprise is opted out by default), and that Mistral Studio’s free mode may use data for training. For Studio and the API, the opt-out is in the Admin Panel under Privacy, and opting out of one product does not opt you out of another. For Labs and Public Preview models, the opt-out does not apply.
Retention: we did not find a default retention period on Mistral’s own pages. Zero data retention exists for some API requests on pay-as-you-go and each request is reviewed. The page lists Agents, Conversations, Files, Chat and Vibe as excluded (we could not tell whether “Chat” means Le Chat or chat requests). The same page says you do not need zero retention to opt out of model training, so retention and training are separate settings.
Location: the global API endpoint does not commit to an inference location. The EU endpoint (api.eu.mistral.ai) is documented as running in EU and EFTA data centers, so a European location needs that endpoint chosen on purpose. We did not confirm where Le Chat or Vibe run.
Not checked: Le Chat’s own privacy page (only a search summary was seen), Mistral’s privacy policy, and any other vendor’s tools.

The open-weight Mistral models (for example ministral-3:8b, Apache 2.0 per Ollama’s page) can run locally through Ollama, where the same local-model caveat applies as for any other: prompts stay on your machine, and tool or web calls may still send data out.
Habits:

Keep unpublished ideas, results and sequences out of consumer chat tools unless the terms say how your text is used and you accept that.
Prefer an agreement your institution has reviewed. Ask your data steward or research office what is approved. They can give advice on contracts and ownership. This quest gives none.
Consider a local model. Ollama says it does not see your prompts or data when you run locally (see Adopt the Pet). Tools and web calls the model makes may still send data out. A free hosted tier is not local: see Free Is Not Free.
Date-stamp your work. A preprint, a repository tag or a dated lab notebook entry records when you had it.
Share on a need-to-know basis. Send collaborators what they need for the task.

title: Who Said What
text:
Prerequisites: The Context Window. This is an optional side quest. Objective: tell the system prompt, the instructions file and your own message apart, and know which you control and which only advise. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code glossary, memory and how-it-works docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/fundamentals.md). Other tools arrange this differently; the ideas carry over. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
When an agent follows a rule, it is fair to ask where that rule came from. There are three common sources, and they differ in who writes them, how long they last and whether anything enforces them.

title: Who Said What
text:
The three voices









Voice
Who writes it
How long it lasts
Can you edit it?




System prompt
The harness
Sent ahead of the conversation on every request
Rarely; you can append or replace it with flags


Instructions file (CLAUDE.md)
You or your team
Loaded at the start of every session
Yes


Your message
You, now
This task
