In Claude Code, the docs describe the system prompt as the instructions sent ahead of your conversation on every request: how to use tools, behave safely and format answers. You can add to it with --append-system-prompt or replace it with --system-prompt.
The instructions file is different from what many people assume. The docs say CLAUDE.md is loaded at the start of every session as a user message after the system prompt (text the model receives in the user’s role). It sits outside the system prompt. Output-style instructions (a setting that changes how the model words its replies) are delivered the same way. Both arrive in the conversation as system reminders (notes the harness slips into the conversation).

title: Who Said What
text:
Rules you did not write
System reminders also carry the skills list, hook additionalContext (text a hook hands back for the harness to add to the conversation), notes about changed files and commit or pull-request attribution lines. If the agent follows a rule you never wrote, for example adding a co-author line to commits, look at what the harness adds on its own first.

title: Who Said What
text:
Advice, not enforcement
The docs say the instructions file is context. Specific and short instructions are followed more consistently, and longer files use more context and reduce adherence. If an action must be blocked regardless of what the model decides, the docs point to a PreToolUse hook (a hook that runs at the point just before a tool runs), which is code that enforces the rule.
We do not know from the docs how the model weighs system prompt against user message internally, so which one wins is left open here. For what must never happen, use enforcement: a hook or a deny rule.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Reads CLAUDE.md. If a project has only an AGENTS.md (and no CLAUDE.md in or above the working directory), it is read instead, from v2.1.277 per the docs. To share one file, import it from CLAUDE.md with @AGENTS.md.


Not checked: OpenCode’s instruction-file loading rules (which names, in what order). Check its own documentation before relying on it.




Pick one behaviour of your agent that you did not expect. Decide whether it came from the harness, your instructions file, or your message. Say how you could tell.


Check your instructions file’s length. If it is long, cut one line that is vague or duplicated.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Prerequisites: Memory, Sessions and Usage. Objective: name the signals that say “start a new session”, the signals that say “carry on”, and when the middle path (compacting) fits better than either. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): research/session-management.md sources on 2026-11-16 (Claude Code best-practices, context-window, sessions and commands docs; OpenCode TUI docs). Claude Code specific unless stated. The cache-and-break numbers come from a community repo (research/cache-and-usage.md), small samples, not run here. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
You have a conversation open with an agent. It has read files, tried things and been corrected. Do you keep typing into it, or start over? Each answer fits some situations, and a wrong choice costs something either way. This page offers signals to weigh.
A few words first. A session is one saved conversation with the tool. Its context is the text the model can see right now (the context window, from The Context Window quest). Compacting means replacing the long history with a short summary and carrying on in the same conversation. Starting fresh means a new, empty conversation. Nothing else changes: your files stay as they are.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Signals to start fresh

A new, unrelated task. The docs recommend /clear between unrelated tasks. They say it costs nothing, and the next task stops paying for the previous one’s history. A session holding three unrelated tasks re-reads all three on every turn (one prompt from you plus the model’s reply) of the fourth. (/clear starts a new empty conversation. Giving it a name, as in /clear oauth-migration, labels the one you leave so you can find it again.)
The agent repeats a wrong claim after two corrections. The docs’ advice is to clear and write one better prompt that includes what you learned. A third correction adds to a conversation that already holds two failed attempts. See Memory, Sessions and Usage.
You notice it forgetting early instructions or contradicting itself. General practice: treat this as a symptom of a crowded or degraded context and start fresh, with the instruction moved into the instructions file. The docs back the underlying mechanism: Anthropic calls the loss of accuracy and recall as context grows context rot, and notes that after compaction, detailed early instructions may be lost. They give no number at which either begins.
You have been away for a while and the next task is new. The harness keeps a cache, a short-term store that makes re-reading the conversation cheaper. Per the docs it lasts about an hour on a subscription and five minutes with an API key. Idle compaction is documented together with the one-hour cache: a very long session (past about 200 thousand tokens) that sits idle may be compacted shortly before the cache expires, so you return to a summary. The docs add: if you do not need the history at all, a fresh session still costs less. If you do need it, resume or carry on (see the table).
The context is crowded. Run /context: it shows what fills the window, with suggestions and capacity warnings. A crowded window with a task you still need is a reason to compact (below); a crowded window full of dead ends is a reason to clear.
A task is finished and a verified result is committed. The result lives in your files and in git, so the conversation has done its job. The docs make the same move after a spec: write it down (the spec: a written description of what to build), then start a fresh session to build from it, so the build begins with a clean context and a written definition of done.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Signals to carry on

Same task, and early decisions still matter. The next step needs the same files, the decisions you made and what was already tried. That is the rule of thumb in this site’s research (our inference from the docs).
The agent is on track. Nothing is being repeated or contradicted. A working session is worth keeping, since clearing it throws away good context.
You are returning to a named session. /resume (or claude --resume <name>) reopens a session you chose; claude --continue reopens the most recent one in this directory. Resume restores the messages, model and permission mode (what the agent may do without asking), and leaves startup flags such as --mcp-config for you to pass again. If that session was compacted, it continues from the last summary.
The tool offers to resume after a long break. On some plans a dialog estimates how much of your usage limit the saved conversation alone would use, and lets you resume or start a new conversation. The docs’ advice: choose by whether your next task still needs the saved conversation.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
The middle path: compact
/compact replaces the history with a summary and stays in the same conversation. Give it a focus note, as in the docs’ example /compact focus on the auth bug fix, so the summary spends its words on what you still need.
What the summary keeps and loses, per the docs: it keeps your requests and key code snippets, but detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost. Afterwards the tool re-supplies the system prompt, the project-root CLAUDE.md, auto memory and skill descriptions, and re-reads up to five recently used files. The docs note that the tool also compacts automatically as you approach the limit. A manual /compact with a focus lets you choose the moment and the emphasis. It costs usage, since compacting itself reads the whole conversation once.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
The decision ladder








Situation
Action
Why




New task, unrelated to this conversation
/clear
Old history would be re-read for nothing, and it can distract


Same task, context crowded, early decisions still matter
/compact with a focus note
Keeps the thread, drops the bulk (details from early on may be lost, so restate any that matter)


Same task, agent on track, plenty of room
Carry on
Nothing to fix


Wrong claim repeated after two corrections
/clear, then one new prompt with what you learned
A third correction sits on top of two failed attempts


Back after a long break, still need the conversation
/resume or claude --continue
You get the saved messages (or the last summary)


Back after a long break, next task is new
Fresh session
Docs: a fresh session still costs less if you do not need the history


Leaving a long session past the cache lifetime, same task afterwards
/compact with a focus note before you leave
Compacting while the cache is warm is cheap; after it expires the history is re-sent at full price (community numbers, small samples)


Task done, verified result committed
Write down what matters, then /clear
The state is in your files and git, not in the chat

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Before you clear
Starting fresh drops the conversation. Your files and memory remain, and the instructions file (CLAUDE.md) and auto memory load again in the new session. Anything you only said in chat is gone: the decisions, what failed and why, which sample misbehaved. General practice: write that down before you clear, because /clear drops the conversation, and commit the result so the state is recoverable. The Handoff Notes quest shows what such a note should contain. If you clear by mistake, /resume can reopen the old conversation.

title: When to Start Fresh
section: The cache and the coffee break
text:
The cache and the coffee break
Signal 4 deserves a closer look, because the cost of a break can be larger than people expect. While the cache is warm, the long history you already sent is re-read cheaply. When the cache has expired, the next request pays to send the whole history again at full price. The docs give the lifetimes: about an hour on a subscription, five minutes with an API key. You can check which one you have with /usage (a “Prompt cache” line is reported there; Not checked: whether it appears on every plan).
A community project, claude-code-usage-analysis, measured this on an API key with a five-minute cache. Treat its numbers as one person’s small experiment (a handful of runs, one model, units that are not a subscription bill; the author lists these limits too). With about 97 thousand tokens of history and a small next fix:







Pause before the next message
Reported cost, compared with a brand-new session




2 to 4 minutes (cache warm)
about 1.5 times


6 to 13 minutes (cache expired)
about 9.8 times



The same project reported that compacting before the break, while the cache is warm, cost about 2.5 times a new session, and compacting after the break cost about as much as simply carrying on. On a subscription, the same cliff should sit near the one-hour mark instead (General practice, our reading of the docs: the project’s own one-hour figure came from a simulator, not a live run).
What this suggests for your habits (General practice, from the numbers above and the docs):

Before a long break in a long session, either /compact with a focus note while the cache is warm, or write a short handoff note and plan to /clear.
After a break, when the next task is new, start fresh. Resuming a long, cold conversation is the expensive path.
After a break, when you still need the thread, a short hand-written note (goal, what is done, what is next) in a new session is often cheaper than re-reading the cold history, and gives you a chance to drop dead ends. The Handoff Notes quest shows what to write.
Short pauses are fine. A few minutes away costs little, so there is no need to rush back.

The same project reported two cost traps worth knowing, both from very small tests: turning a built-in tool off in the middle of a task made the next turn cost roughly twenty times a normal one, since the cache was thrown away, while editing CLAUDE.md, adding an MCP server or changing effort showed no such jump. Decide your tool set at the start of a task. It also reported that a long log left in the chat added to the cost of every later turn. Trim output before it lands in the conversation, for example by asking the agent to show only the last lines or a pass/fail summary.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
The cost of both mistakes
Clearing too early loses useful context. The agent must re-read files and rediscover decisions, which costs time and usage, and you may need to repeat yourself. Clearing too late costs too: the whole conversation is sent again on every request, so usage climbs, and per the docs a focused context gives better answers than a crowded one, even with a large window. Both errors are cheap to recover from if you wrote things down. That is the argument for notes. Not checked: the default auto-compact threshold (the docs defer to a model-configuration page we did not read), so this page gives no percentage to aim for.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands the docs confirm for this page: /clear (alias /new), /compact [instructions], /context, /resume [session], claude --continue, claude --resume [name], /rename. To check how full the window is, use /context. Not checked: whether the status line (the strip of information below the prompt) can show a context-fullness figure.


The OpenCode terminal-interface docs list /new (alias /clear), /sessions (aliases /resume, /continue) and /compact (alias /summarize). Not checked: what OpenCode keeps or loses when it compacts, whether it has a /context-style display, and how a local Ollama model’s smaller window changes the advice. General practice: the same signals apply to any tool, because every model has a finite window; expect to start fresh sooner with a smaller one.




Next time you notice yourself pasting the same background twice, note it: that was the moment to put it in the instructions file.


At the end of your next working session, write one line saying which signal (new task, repeated error, forgotten instruction, long break, crowded context, finished and committed) would have told you to start fresh, or that none applied.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
Prerequisites: Know Your Gear. Objective: explain that a model reads tokens (chunks of text), and know which sequence jobs belong to a script. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude API glossary and token-counting docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/fundamentals.md). The DNA examples are general practice and were not measured here. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
You read a read as letters: A, C, G, T. A language model reads tokens. Before your text reaches the model, it is cut into tokens, and the model works with those.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
What a token is
Anthropic’s glossary describes tokens as the smallest units a model works with. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, a single character or a byte. Common strings get larger tokens because that is efficient. Rare or unseen words are broken into smaller pieces so the model can still handle them.
Three consequences:

Tokens are not words. A sentence of ten words rarely comes to ten tokens; the count depends on the model and the language.
The count changes between models. The docs say newer tokenizers (the part that cuts text into tokens) can produce about 30 percent more tokens for the same text, for Claude 4.7 and later, including Sonnet 5.5. So count again for each model generation.
Limits and cost are measured in tokens. The context window is counted in tokens, and the docs frame cost in tokens too: the same prompt can cost different amounts on different models. The API (programmatic access to the model, billed per token, as opposed to a chat plan) has a free token-counting endpoint, and its answer is an estimate that may differ slightly from real use.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
Why this matters for sequences
The model sees chunks of letters. As general practice (we found no official page that says this about DNA), expect these problems:

A DNA string is not read one base per token. It is cut into chunks of several letters that follow no biological rule.
Counting letters (“how many Gs in this read”) means counting inside chunks the model cannot see into. Answers are often close and sometimes wrong.
Copying exactly a long string, retyping a barcode or an accession, can drop or swap a character without any sign.
Positions, reverse complements and checksums depend on every single letter.

So the rule: if the answer has to be exact and a rule for it exists, have the agent run a script or a tool and report what it printed. Check any sequence the model retyped against the source file.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Ask it to write and run the counting command and read its output. You can then read the command and the output yourself.


Same advice. Small local models tend to be less reliable at exact tasks, so the case for running code is even stronger (general practice).

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
Optional exercise (laptop, no real data)
Take this mock line, which is not real data: >read1 ACGTTGCAAGGCTTAGGCCATTAGC. Count the letters yourself with a command you already have, for example echo ACGTTGCAAGGCTTAGGCCATTAGC | grep -o G | wc -l. Then paste the same line and a plain English sentence of similar length into any tokenizer page you trust, or a token counter you have. Compare the token counts. Keep real or sensitive sequences out of web tools.

Compare the token count of a mock FASTA line and an English sentence of the same character length, using a tool you trust and only mock data. Note which one used more tokens.


Replace one “ask the model to count” habit of yours with a script the model writes and runs, and check its output against a hand count on a tiny file.

title: The Context Window
text:
Prerequisites: Tokens, Not Letters. Objective: say what fills the context window, what happens when it is full, and three habits that keep it useful. Time: about 20 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude API context-windows docs and Claude Code context-window and how-it-works docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/fundamentals.md). Compaction details are Claude Code specific. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
The context window is all the text the model can look at when it writes its next piece of output, including its own reply. Anthropic’s docs compare it to working memory, and say it is separate from what the model learned in training. It is measured in tokens, as in the last quest.

title: The Context Window
text:
What fills it
In Claude Code the docs list: your instructions, the files it reads, its own responses, and content that never appears in your terminal. Before you type anything, the window already holds the instructions file (CLAUDE.md, the text file the harness loads at session start; see Know Your Gear), auto memory, the names of MCP tools and skill descriptions. Every file it reads and every tool output then adds more. At the API level (programmatic access to the model) the same idea holds: system prompt (the harness’s own instructions, sent with every request), every message, tool results, tool definitions and the output all count.
Sizes depend on the model, up to 1 million tokens for some and 200 thousand for others, per the docs. A big window gives room for more text, and quality depends on what fills it.

title: The Context Window
text:
Bigger is not better
Anthropic’s docs put it directly: as the token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade. They call this context rot. The docs give no number at which it starts, so treat any quoted figure without a source as unverified. The practical point: what you put in matters as much as how much fits.

title: The Context Window
text:
When it fills up

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


It compacts automatically as the limit nears: the history is replaced by a summary. The docs say the summary keeps your requests and key code snippets, but detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost. What is re-supplied afterwards: the system prompt, the project-root CLAUDE.md, auto memory and skill descriptions; up to five recently read or edited files are read again (a file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path only). Nested instruction files are summarised away and reload on demand.
Useful controls: /context shows what is using space, /compact with a focus note compacts on purpose, /clear starts clean between unrelated tasks. A subagent (a helper agent) has its own window and only a summary comes back. If one file or output is so big that the window refills after every summary, auto-compaction stops with an error.


Not checked: OpenCode’s compaction behaviour. Compaction is documented here for Claude Code only. General practice: expect any tool to drop or summarise something when the window is full, and a local model often runs with a smaller window, so check your model’s setting and how your tool reports usage.

title: The Context Window
text:
Three habits

Start fresh for a new task. An unrelated earlier thread takes room and can distract (general practice).
Keep outputs small. In bioinformatics terms: ask for the head, a count, or a summary script’s output when the file is a big variant table or a whole log (general practice).
Put durable facts in the instructions file, such as how to run tests or which folders are off limits. Instructions given only in chat can be lost to compaction. Keep that file short; Anthropic’s docs target under 200 lines and say longer files use more context and reduce adherence.


In a session you already have, look at what is using the window (in Claude Code, run /context). Note the largest item and whether you chose it.


Find one instruction you keep retyping in chat and move it into your instructions file in one short line.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
Prerequisites: The Context Window. Objective: use six terms precisely (token, context window, session context, memory, session usage, context poisoning), and say what to do when a wrong claim has got into a session or into memory. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): research/failure-modes.md sources on 2026-11-16 (Claude Code memory, sessions, costs, commands and best-practices docs). Claude Code specific unless stated. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
People say “it remembers”, “the session got long” and “I hit my usage” as if these were one thing. They are different things, with different places they live and different ways to reset them. Think of a lab glossary: one term, one meaning.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
The glossary
Token. A chunk of text the model reads (a word piece, a character or a byte). Context limits and usage are counted in tokens. Details are in Tokens, Not Letters.
Context window. Everything the model can see when it writes its next output. It has a size limit, measured in tokens. See The Context Window.
Session and session context. A session is a saved conversation tied to a project directory (stored locally as a transcript file). Its session context is what is in the window right now. The docs say each session begins with a fresh context window and that sessions are independent: a new session has no history from earlier ones.
Memory. Text on disk that is read into a new window at the start of every session. In Claude Code there are two kinds, both loaded at session start:

CLAUDE.md: instructions you write (scope = who or where a setting applies: project, user or organisation).
Auto memory: notes the harness writes itself from your corrections and preferences. It is per git repository and machine-local, kept in ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/ as plain markdown with a MEMORY.md index. Only the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md load at start; topic files are read on demand.

Memory is advisory context, and it takes room in the window every session. Run /clear and the conversation goes while memory stays. Compaction shrinks a session and leaves memory as it was.
Session usage. How much of your allowance a session consumes. In Claude Code, /usage shows an estimated session cost (worked out locally from token counts at list price, the published per-token price), plan usage limits and activity stats. /cost and /stats are aliases. The displayed session total resets on /clear; whether allowance already spent on a plan comes back is not documented (our inference: it does not). Two billing worlds exist: with a subscription, the plan bars are what matter and the dollar figure is an estimate (plans have rolling and weekly limit windows; see your plan docs, as the docs we read confirm the exact windows only for Teams and Enterprise per-seat allowances); with the API, usage is billed per token, and thinking tokens (the tokens the model spends reasoning before it answers) count as output tokens. The docs do not state allowance sizes for the individual plans, so see the vendor’s pricing page.
Context poisoning. A wrong or injected statement enters the context and later answers build on it. This is a community term from outside vendor documentation. It was coined in the post “How Long Contexts Fail” (2025-06-22) credited to Drew Breunig (the byline comes from a reprint listing; the page text we read did not name him). His example is a game-playing agent whose recorded goals became corrupted with false state. We found no use of this term in Anthropic’s docs; they do describe the same trap in plain words, below.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
Why usage climbs
The docs give these reasons. Claude Code sends the whole conversation on every request, and each tool-using step is another request. Caching (a short-term store so repeated text is cheaper to re-read) makes re-reading cheaper but a short question late in a long session still draws on all of it. Large tool outputs (the docs’ example is reading a 10,000-line log) stay in the conversation. Subagents each have their own context, and their requests still count. /compact itself reads the whole conversation. Remedies from the docs: /clear between unrelated tasks, /compact with a focus note, /context to see what fills the window, and keeping CLAUDE.md under 200 lines.
The cache has a lifetime, and a long break can outlast it, which makes the next message much dearer. When to Start Fresh has a section on the cache and the coffee break, with a community measurement (small sample, labelled as such).
Seeing “rate limited until …” in /usage means the tool could not fetch plan limits, and says nothing about your work being limited.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
section: When a wrong claim gets in
text:
When a wrong claim gets in
Anthropic’s best-practices guidance is plain: if you have corrected the same thing twice and it is still wrong, /clear plus one new prompt that folds in what you learned works well, since a third correction mostly adds to a conversation that already holds two failed attempts for the model to re-read. /rewind can roll back to before the bad turn.
Memory persists, so a wrong line costs the most there. General practice (our inference, from no official instruction): do not let a claim into CLAUDE.md or auto memory until you have checked it against the source, such as the data, the tool’s --help or the paper. If a bad line is already there, open /memory, read what has been written about your project, and delete it.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands the docs confirm: /memory (lists memory files, toggles auto memory, opens the folder), /clear (new empty conversation; the old one stays resumable), /compact, /resume and claude --resume (pick an earlier session), claude --continue (most recent in this directory), /usage, /context. Resume restores messages, model and permission mode (what the agent may do without asking), and leaves startup flags such as --mcp-config for you to pass again. Transcripts are deleted after 30 days by default.


Not checked: OpenCode’s memory files, session commands and usage reporting. The research for this page covers Claude Code only. General practice: with a local Ollama model the window is still finite, so the ideas about session context and poisoned claims carry over; find your tool’s own commands in its documentation. Not checked: whether anything is billed per token by a vendor.




If you use a tool with memory, open it (in Claude Code, /memory) and read what it has recorded about a project. Is every line something you could source?


In a session you already have, run /usage and note what dominates: long conversation, big outputs or subagents. If it is not available to you, skip this.

title: Handoff Notes
text:
Prerequisites: The Stream of Ideas. Objective: say what a fresh session knows (nothing about your task except what loads automatically or is written down), list the five things that carry knowledge across the gap, and write a short handoff note a fresh session can act on, with what was checked kept separate from what was not. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): research/session-management.md sources on 2026-11-16. Claude Code specific unless stated. Handoff-note contents are general practice; there is no official template. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
You stop work on Friday with a half-finished refactor. On Monday you open a new session (one conversation with the agent, which has its own context: the text it can see right now). Claude Code’s docs say each session begins with a fresh context window. Anthropic’s article on long-running agents says the same in other words: a new session begins with no memory of what came before. So the new session does not know your goal, what you tried, or what you checked. Anything it should know has to cross the gap in writing.

title: Handoff Notes
section: Five things that cross the gap
text:
Five things that cross the gap

The instructions file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code). A file you write that is loaded at the start of every session. Good for stable facts and conventions: how to run the tests, which folders are off limits.
Auto memory. Notes the harness writes itself, from your corrections and preferences. In Claude Code, /memory lists and opens them. See Memory, Sessions and Usage for both kinds of memory.
Files in the repository (the project folder under version control): code, tests, a README, and, if you keep one, a progress or handoff file.
Git history. A commit is a saved snapshot of the project with a message you or the agent write. The list of commits shows what changed and when. It is durable unless rewritten (rebase, amend, force-push), and unpushed commits are local only (general practice).
Your handoff note. A short file about the state of one task, written for the next session. This is general practice. We found no official Claude Code page that prescribes a handoff file or its location, so the structure below is ours.











What
Goes where

Who writes it

Stable rules and conventions

Every session until you edit it
You

Memory the tool wrote can be wrong, and a wrong line is loaded again every session. That is the trap called context poisoning, explained in Memory, Sessions and Usage. Check any claim against the source before you rely on it.
Anthropic’s engineering article “Effective harnesses for long-running agents” describes a similar set of habits (our paraphrase): keep a progress notes file, make git commits with descriptive messages so bad changes can be reverted, and begin each session with a startup routine that reads the progress file and the recent git log, then runs a basic check before new work.

title: Handoff Notes
section: What a good handoff note contains
text:
What a good handoff note contains
General practice; there is no official format. Keep it short, so reading it costs less than rediscovering the state. Point to files and commands, and let the next session run them for fresh output.

Goal in one line.
Current state: branch, last commit, what runs and what does not.
Decisions and the reasons, including options you rejected.
Verified, and how; not verified. Two separate lists. For each verified item, the command and what it showed.
What failed and should not be retried.
Next steps, in order.
Pointers: file paths, commands, job IDs, work directories.
Open questions and parked ideas (see The Stream of Ideas).

title: Handoff Notes
text:
Mock example
This is a mock handoff note for a mock task. The file names and numbers are invented.
# HANDOFF: qc_filter.py refactor (mock example)

## Goal
Replace the per-read loop in qc_filter.py with a vectorised version, same output.

## State (git branch refactor-qc, last commit a1b2c3d "qc: add vectorised mean quality")
- New function mean_qual_fast() is written and called from main().
- Old function mean_qual() is kept for comparison. Do not delete yet.

## Decisions
- Keep both functions until all samples are compared (a bug here would silently change which reads pass).
- Threshold stays at mean Q20, as in the lab protocol.

## Verified
- tests/test_filter.py: ran `pytest -q`, 6 passed.
- sample_A: `diff <(python qc_filter.py A.fq) old_out/A.txt` gave no output.

## Not verified
- Samples B and C have not been compared with the old output.
- Reads shorter than 30 bases: no test covers them.
- Speed gain: not measured.

## Failed, do not retry
- Using numpy on the raw quality string: wrong values for the Phred offset. Convert to integers first.

## Next steps
1. Compare B and C against old_out/ with the same diff command.
2. Add a test for a 10-base read.
3. Only then delete mean_qual().

## Open questions / parked
- Should the threshold be a command-line option? Parked for a later task.

title: Handoff Notes
section: Where to put it, and how to start the next session
text:
Where to put it, and how to start the next session
Put the note in a file the next session can find. Two options (general practice): a file in the repo, such as HANDOFF.md, if the team should see it; or a gitignored ordinary file you point to if it is personal, which is the simpler choice. CLAUDE.local.md at the project root (added to .gitignore, loaded after CLAUDE.md) is the only guidance we found on keeping personal per-project notes out of git, and it is meant for preferences; per the research it exists only in the worktree where it was created. Anything loaded every session takes room in the window, which is why the parking lot in The Stream of Ideas is kept out of it, and a finished handoff note is best taken out of it. Not checked: whether CLAUDE.local.md suits short-lived task notes better than an ordinary file you point to.
Write the note before you run /clear (which starts a new empty conversation), because /clear drops the conversation (general practice). Pairing the note with a commit leaves a matching record in git.
Then start the new session with a prompt like this:

Read HANDOFF.md, then tell me your understanding before changing anything.

The agent restates the goal and state in its own words, and you compare that with what you know. This is a cheap comprehension check (general practice): it can catch a misreading of the note. The restatement comes from the same model that read it, so the note’s claims still need checking against the source. Checking claims against the source is the idea behind Ground Truth (later in the Maze).
You can ask the agent to draft the note at the end of a session. A good habit is to review it yourself, since a draft can overstate what was verified (“all tests pass” when none were run in that session).

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands the research confirms: /memory (see memory files), /clear (new empty conversation), /resume and claude --resume (reopen an earlier session), claude --continue (most recent session in this directory), /export (writes the conversation as plain text for a person to read). There is no documented /handoff or /save command. Not checked: whether /export output makes a good handoff; transcripts are long, so a short curated note is probably better (our inference).


Not checked: OpenCode’s memory files and how it loads project instructions. The research confirms these OpenCode commands: /new (alias /clear), /sessions (aliases /resume and /continue), /compact and /export. The handoff note itself is just a file, so the practice carries over. Not checked: how a local model with a small window copes with a long note, so keep it short.




Write a handoff note for a task you are on and give it to a fresh session with the prompt above. Does its restatement match your own?


Ask an agent to draft a handoff note, then mark each line in your own words as checked by you, or not checked. Count how many lines it overstated.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
Prerequisites: Grow the Carapace. Objective: keep heavy work and sprawling searches off the shared login node and shared storage, and hand heavy work to the scheduler. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Slurm, Claude Code and OpenCode (V2) docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/hpc-and-notebooks.md)
Everything below that concerns etiquette is general practice: the Slurm documentation does not define login nodes, and your site’s rules differ. Follow your own cluster’s policy and user guide over this page. This page makes no claim that using an LLM agent on a cluster is allowed or expected. Ask your cluster staff first (see Keys on Shared Ground). This quest is read-only. Do not run the exercise on a real cluster.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
Login node versus compute node
General practice. A login node is shared by everyone who logs in. Compute nodes are where the scheduler places your jobs. Light work (editing text, git, listing one directory, checking a log with head or tail) is normally fine on the login node. Heavy work belongs on compute nodes: aligners, long foreground pipelines, compressing or indexing big files, building large environments, or running a test suite at scale.
An agent does not know which node it is on or what your site tolerates. It will happily run a long command if you let it, so the rule is yours to set. It also misjudges “this will only take a few seconds”, so when a command’s cost is unclear, tell it to ask.
Some sites forbid agents on login nodes altogether, or allow them only inside an interactive compute allocation (where internet access may be restricted). Ask your staff before you start one. Your site may run a different scheduler, with its own submission syntax, partitions and accounting. If a scheduler command is missing, ask staff rather than trying near-matches.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
Shared storage prefers scoped searches
General practice. Network filesystems can slow down for everyone when something touches huge numbers of files. Agents explore by searching, so a careless find / or a recursive grep -r from your home or project root is the classic mistake. Ask for searches scoped to one known directory, and keep them away from /. The same goes for du, ls --recursive, ls --format=long (it stats every file) and wide globs on big directories, and avoid making many small files in one directory. Keep the agent to your own project paths: other users’ or other projects’ paths are off limits unless you named them or the site documents them as shared (reference data).
Claude Code’s own search tools (Glob, Grep) are file tools, and its documentation does not describe them as a control on filesystem load. Scoping the search is on you.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
The scheduler’s four commands
From the Slurm documentation:







Command
What it is for




sbatch
submit a job script for later execution. It returns once the script has a job ID


srun
run a job or job step in real time. If needed it first creates a resource allocation


squeue
report the state of jobs


scancel
cancel a pending or running job



sbatch --test-only validates a script and estimates a start time, and “No job is actually submitted”. That makes it a dry run, in the same spirit as the Factory’s Dry Run First. Slurm’s default time limit is the partition’s default, so set limits in the script.
General practice: set --time, --mem and --cpus-per-task, and use a job array for many similar tasks. Write options in their long form (--dry-run for -n) so you can read what the agent proposes.
Resources are billed by what is allocated, whatever is used. If --mem is more than the CPUs you asked for allow (partition limit MaxMemPerCPU), Slurm may raise the CPU count to fit, with no error. It can also reject the job instead. Per the sbatch page, --mem-per-cpu above that limit is reduced and --cpus-per-task raised to compensate. Read the limits with scontrol show partition <name>, and afterwards compare request, allocation and use with sacct --jobs=<id> --format=JobID,State,ReqMem,AllocCPUS,MaxRSS. A job killed for memory shows OUT_OF_MEMORY, often with exit code 0:125 (tools report 137); MaxRSS then understates the need, so raise the request above the failed one. Not checked: the 0:125 code and the --mem widening rule against the Slurm pages.
Scratch means throwaway files. Ask where the project’s scratch is. Choose the project’s scratch over /tmp, which is shared on a login node and often small. A set $TMPDIR is no proof of scratch (Slurm can set it to /tmp). Scripts, logs and final outputs stay in the project directory.
Before a copy or a delete, find out what it touches. Run rsync --dry-run --itemize-changes first, with the same arguments, and read the list. cp, scp and rm have no dry run, so list the exact path or glob and delete only those names. Send large transfers through the scheduler or the site’s data-transfer node. The Factory’s Dry Run First is the same habit.

title: Login Node Manners
section: What the agent’s sandbox does and does not cover
text:
What the agent’s sandbox does and does not cover

Claude Code’s sandbox is shell-only. File tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it.
It fails open by default: if it cannot start, commands run without sandboxing, unless sandbox.failIfUnavailable is true. On Linux it needs bubblewrap and socat. General practice: you usually cannot install packages system-wide on a cluster yourself, so a site may have to provide them. Whether it works there is site-specific.
So “the sandbox is on” is something to check.


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Tell the agent where it may run what, in your project instructions or the prompt, and back it with a permission rule where you can (see Jobs, Not Jam). Useful instructions:

“Search only inside ./workflow/. Never run find or grep -r from / or $HOME.”
“Run nothing in the foreground on the login node. Draft an sbatch script and show it to me.”

Instructions are guidance only. If a project instruction file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) is stricter than a generic skill or these lines, the stricter one wins.
From the Claude Code docs: foreground commands time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default), so a long-running foreground command in the agent’s shell is cut off anyway.


The same habits apply. OpenCode’s documented permission model (V2 docs; check your installed version) ends with allow, ask or deny rules, and an unmatched action asks. Per the docs the base policy begins with an allow-all rule, so sbatch is likely to run unprompted; confirm in your version. Add explicit rules for the cluster commands; the default alone is a weak guard. A local model through Ollama leaves the node you are on and the filesystem behaviour as they are.

text:
Prerequisites: Login Node Manners. Objective: let the agent draft job scripts while you keep submitting and cancelling under your own approval, and know what polling costs. Time: about 20 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Slurm, Claude Code and OpenCode (V2) docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/hpc-and-notebooks.md)
Whether an agent should be anywhere near your cluster account is a decision for you and your cluster staff. Follow your own cluster’s policy and data agreement over this page. This page makes no claim that agent use is allowed or expected on any cluster. Read this quest on your laptop. Do not try the rules on a real cluster.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Draft versus submit
A job script is text. Letting an agent draft one is low risk, because you read it before anything runs. Submitting spends shared resources, and cancelling can destroy work. A sensible split:

the agent drafts scripts, and may check state (squeue, sinfo, sacct). General practice: limit sacct with --jobs=<jobid> or --starttime=<date> so it does not dump the whole accounting history
you approve sbatch, srun, salloc and scancel

Before approving an sbatch, read the script and the resource request: --time, --mem, and the array size if it is an array.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
Jobs, Not Jam
section: Why scancel -u is the dangerous one
text:
Why scancel -u is the dangerous one
scancel -u <you> signals all your jobs, including ones the agent did not submit. Whole jobs are terminated, and other work of yours dies with them. scancel --me does the same in a longer spelling. The man page lists more bulk selectors too: --name, --state, --partition, plus account, QOS, reservation and node list. Each acts on every job it matches, and combined filters must all match. Denying a few spellings cannot cover them all, so the single ask rule on scancel * is the net, and the deny rules catch the worst two. Prefer scancel <jobid> for an ID the agent itself submitted. Slurm can also rate-limit requests per user when they come in at a sustained high rate, so a runaway loop of commands is a problem for the scheduler as well as for you.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Polling costs money, and attention
Claude Code charges by token use. The whole conversation is sent with every request, and each tool use sends another request. A /loop (a command that re-runs a prompt on a timer) that polls squeue keeps firing on its interval, even while the session is idle, and sends your full context each time. Verbose output such as long logs also inflates the context.
The scheduler pays too. The squeue and sacct pages warn against running them from loops: it can slow slurmctld (the scheduler daemon) or slurmdbd (the accounting database) for everyone.
General practice (the site owner’s own skill, research/hpc-and-notebooks.md):

Poll no more than about once a minute, less often for long jobs. Run one loop at a time and scope it: squeue --user=$USER or --jobs=<id>.
Prefer sbatch --parsable --wait, or the pipeline’s own poller, to a sleep loop. This replaces a /loop of squeue, so skip the loop.
A wait can outlast the tool’s timeout. Run it in the background. Never resubmit because the wait timed out; check State with sacct first: --wait passes the job’s exit code through, but a signal-killed job gives 1, so the code alone is a poor proof of success.
Submit many similar tasks as one array with a concurrency cap (--array=1-100%10) instead of a loop of sbatch calls.

From the Claude Code docs: foreground commands time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default), so an agent waiting on a long foreground command, such as an srun that blocks until it finishes, gets cut off.

title: Name the Fears
text: Prerequisites: none. Objective: name what worries you about large language model (LLM) agents (an agent is a model running inside a program that picks and runs tools in a loop toward a goal), and learn the habit that answers each worry. Time: about 10 minutes. General practice, not a vendor claim: nothing here depends on a tool version.

title: Name the Fears
text:
Why start with fears
You do not have to like these tools. Many careful people in science are wary of them, and most of the wariness is reasonable. This odyssey keeps your worries and gives each one a habit that makes the risk smaller, so you can decide with your eyes open.
Each worry below is a real enemy in this land. Each has a counter-habit, and the rest of the odyssey trains them.









The worry
The enemy
The counter-habit
Where you learn it




“It will stop me learning.”
Learning-drain
Write it first, predict before you look, ask it to explain while you do the work.
Biodiversity Reef


“It produces slop in bulk.”
Slop-ooze
Small steps, tests before code, a review budget.
Sequence Maze


“It makes things up.”
Mirage
Check against something the agent did not write.
Sequence Maze


“Someone else has to review all this.”
Review-leech
Review it yourself first, say that you used an LLM, send small changes.
Biodiversity Reef


“It could delete my work or leak my data.”
Data-wipe
Undo (git), permissions, a sandbox (an operating-system layer that limits what commands can touch) or scratch directory, no secrets in prompts (a prompt is the text you send to the model).
Ancient DNA Crypt


“I do not understand what it did.”
Black-box husk
Ask for a changelog and explain it back before you keep it.
Sequence Maze


“Finishing this with an agent will feel hollow, as if it was not really my work.”
Hollow-victory
Make the decisions, be able to explain each step, keep a short decision log, credit the agent’s part openly.
Biodiversity Reef


“Everyone will expect work to be done faster now.”
Clock-shifter
Say where the time goes, agree timelines that include review, share how long checking took.
Biodiversity Reef


“Everything I write will start to sound the same.”
Echo-bland
Draft the first version in your own words, then edit; keep a style you recognise; use the agent for structure and checks.
Biodiversity Reef


“I will spend my days checking drafts and lose the creative part of my work.”
Draft-warden
Keep the question, the design and the interpretation for yourself; give the agent routine drafting; count checking time as part of the work.
Biodiversity Reef


“People will think I am lazy or unoriginal for using it.”
Side-eye
Say plainly what the agent did and what you checked; follow your team’s norm; let the evidence speak.
Biodiversity Reef


“I will stop trusting my own judgement.”
Doubt-fog
Decide first, then ask for a second opinion; keep a few decisions agent-free; note the times your own call was right.
Biodiversity Reef


“My unpublished results or ideas will leak and someone will get there first.”
Leak-shade
Learn what your tool’s data terms say about retention and training use, keep unpublished work out of consumer chat tools, prefer an agreement your institution has reviewed or a local model, date-stamp your work.
Ancient DNA Crypt



Slop is low-quality bulk output. A review budget means you only produce as much as you can honestly review today.






Note



Sometimes the right answer is to skip the LLM. Part of the skill is knowing when.

Token counting: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it documents the free count endpoint and says models from Claude 4.7 onward use a newer tokenizer, so the same text gives roughly 30 percent more tokens than on earlier models (the exact increase depends on the content). Cited in: Tokens, Not Letters.
The Strawberry Problem: Cosma et al., EMNLP 2025, paper. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Tokens, Not Letters: it argues character-level information is weakly available inside tokens, a leading explanation for miscounted letters.
Ground Truth: it studies why models miscount letters and links it to tokens, which is the idea behind miscounted bases.

Counting Ability of LLMs and Impact of Tokenization: Zhang et al., arXiv, paper. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Tokens, Not Letters: it studies how tokenisation affects counting; its abstract says step-by-step reasoning (chain of thought) can help, and its full text still reports failures with it in modern models. A preprint.
Ground Truth: it shows how tokenisation changes counting accuracy in language models, which is why a script, not a model’s reading, should do exact counts (that last step is our general practice, not the paper’s claim). A preprint.

CharBench: Evaluating the Role of Tokenization in Character-Level Tasks: arXiv, paper. Why read: a counter-view finding tokenisation only weakly tied to errors, so treat the tokens explanation as likely but disputed. A preprint. Cited in: Tokens, Not Letters.
Lost in the Middle: Liu et al., arXiv, paper. Cited by 3 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Where Machines Fail: it shows recall is best for text at the start or end of a long input and weaker in the middle. A preprint.
RAG and Its Cousins: it shows why a long, stuffed prompt can hide the passage that matters.
Boss: The Wall of Output: it measures how accuracy drops when the relevant fact sits in the middle of a long input.

Why read: its abstract says specialised math and coding models still struggle with simple counting and that reasoning before answering is the most reliable fix; its full text adds that explicitly asking coding models for Python code worked. A preprint, not peer-reviewed as far as we checked. Cited in: Where Machines Fail.

title: Know Your Gear
text:
Prerequisites: Three Kinds of Machine. Objective: use the words this site relies on (model, harness, skill, MCP, hook, plugin, effort, eval, and the context terms below) and say how they fit together. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code and API docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/terminology.md, research/failure-modes.md and research/fundamentals.md). Mistral Vibe: its GitHub page and docs read 2026-11-20 through a summarising tool (research/mistral.md). Other tools name things differently; the ideas carry over.
People mix these words up, and the mix-ups cause real mistakes, such as blaming “the model” for something a setting did. In this world the companions are models, and the harness is their armour.

title: Know Your Gear
text:
The picture



How model, harness and extensions relate

A large box labelled harness contains a smaller box labelled model, with an effort dial on the model. Inside the harness are tools, permissions, and the loop with context. A row of extensions sits in the harness: skill, MCP, hook, and plugin which bundles them. Outside the harness an eval measures results by running with and without an extension. To the right, the same model is shown inside two different harnesses.   HARNESS (the armour)  MODEL (companion) reads text, writes text  EFFORT: how much it thinks per step Tools: read, edit Permissions Loop, context EXTENSIONS you plug in SKILL MCP HOOK  PLUGIN: a bundle of the above INSTRUCTIONS  EVAL: run with and without, compare  TWO HARNESSES  Model Xinside harness A  Model Xinside harness B Different tools, permission rules and loop, so the same model can behave differently. Claude Code and OpenCode are two harnesses. 


Models think. The harness decides what they can touch and runs the loop. Extensions change what the harness offers. Evals measure from outside. Text version below.

title: Know Your Gear
text:
The words

Model. The large language model (LLM) that reads and writes text (for example Claude Sonnet 5.5, a Mistral model, or a local model through Ollama, a program that runs models on your own computer). It is not the product you type into. Aliases such as sonnet move to newer versions over time, so pin the full name when a result must be reproducible.
Harness. The program around the model. Per the Claude Code docs it provides the tools, manages the context the model sees, runs the loop (gather context, act, check, repeat) and enforces permissions. Claude Code, OpenCode (an open-source harness) and Mistral Vibe (Mistral’s open-source terminal coding agent) are harnesses. Many questions are really about the harness: what may it touch, what does it remember, what does it ask first?
Prompt. The text you send to the model.
Turn. One prompt from you plus the model’s reply.
Agent. A model inside a harness that picks and runs tools in a loop toward a goal.
Tool. An action the model can request and the harness runs, such as reading a file or running a shell command. A tool call is one such request; tool output is what comes back. (We also say “the tool” for the program you run; see Harness.)
Subagent. A helper agent with its own context window; only its summary comes back.
Instructions file. A text file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, AGENTS.md in OpenCode where read) that the harness loads at session start. It advises; it does not enforce.
Sandbox. An operating-system layer that limits what commands can touch. A scratch folder is a different thing: a throwaway directory.
Hallucination (called a Mirage in the Sequence Maze). A plausible-looking statement that is false, such as an invented DOI (a paper’s permanent identifier).
Prompt injection. Text from a file, web page or tool that the model treats as an instruction.
Skill. A folder with a SKILL.md. Only its short description is preloaded; the body loads when it is used. It advises. (You wrote one in Forge a Skill, later in this world.)
MCP (Model Context Protocol). An open standard for connecting the harness to outside tools and data, such as a database or a literature search. A server you connect can act on your behalf, so treat it like software you install.
Hook. Your own command, request or prompt that the harness runs automatically at a set point, such as before a tool call. A command hook that exits with code 2 before a tool runs stops that action whatever the model wants (a nonzero exit code is how a script signals failure; a hook uses 2 to mean block). A rule in an instructions file can only ask. That is why hooks are the stronger guard.
Plugin. A folder that bundles skills, hooks, MCP servers and more, installed as one unit. It can run code, so it is a trust decision.
Effort. A setting for how much the model reasons per step, from low to max in Claude Code (/effort, --effort; a /command is typed inside the running tool, a --flag when you start it). Low is faster and cheaper; high thinks longer and checks more. It acts as a behavioural signal, with no exact budget behind it. The docs warn that max can show diminishing returns and overthink, so raise it only where you measure a gain. It makes answers more careful, and correctness is still yours to check.
Eval. A repeatable test of agent behaviour: a prompt plus checks on the result. Comparing runs with and without something (a skill, a rule) shows what it contributed. A score of 100% both ways means it contributed nothing.

title: Know Your Gear
section: Words about what the model can see
text:
Words about what the model can see
These get mixed up more than any others. The Codon Mill quests take each one in turn.

Token. The chunk of text a model actually reads and writes. Somewhere between a letter and a word. Limits and costs are counted in tokens. (See Tokens, Not Letters.)
Context window. Everything the model can see at once right now: instructions, files it has read, tool output and the conversation so far. It has a size limit, and a fuller window is not automatically a better one. (See The Context Window.)
Session (session context). One running conversation, and the context window it has built up. A new session starts with an empty conversation. Two sessions do not share their context.
Memory. Notes that the harness loads at the start of every session, such as your instructions file and, in Claude Code, notes the tool writes itself. Memory outlives a session; session context does not. (See Memory, Sessions and Usage.)
Compaction. The harness replaces old conversation with a summary to free room.
Session usage. How much of your allowance or bill a session spends. It climbs with the size of the context, because the whole conversation is sent again with each request.
Context poisoning. A community term, not vendor documentation: a wrong statement gets into the context, and later answers build on it. Starting a fresh session and keeping unverified claims out of memory files are sensible remedies (general practice).







Note



Naming differs between tools. The Claude Code docs define “harness” and “hooks” as above; a good habit is to check another tool’s docs for how its hooks, plugins and effort settings work.



Redraw the picture from memory for the tool you actually use: which model, which harness, which extensions are loaded right now?

title: Three Kinds of Machine
text:
Three kinds

A deterministic program (a script, awk, samtools): the same input always gives the same output, and you can read why. Use it whenever the rule is known.
A trained model (a classifier, a gene-finder, a structure predictor): learned from data to do one task, with measured accuracy on that task. Use it when the rule is unknown but the task is narrow and validated.
A large language model (LLM): trained on large amounts of text, then tuned to follow instructions. Flexible and fluent, with no built-in guarantee of correctness. Use it where the task is open-ended and you can check the result, such as drafting, explaining, or writing a first version of code that you then test.

Two common mistakes: using an LLM to do something a one-line script does exactly (slow, costly, and sometimes wrong), and trusting a model outside the task it was validated for.
An LLM can also be called inside a script (for example to tidy free-text labels). That makes your pipeline non-deterministic, so the result needs its own checks and the exact model and version recorded.
The AI for Science best practices (a European draft, not yet endorsed by any body) start from the same question: before reaching for an agent or a large model, ask whether a script, a fixed workflow or a smaller specialised model does the job. Their reasons are cost and reproducibility: a method that fits the task is often cheaper to run and easier to reproduce, and it does not change when a provider updates a hosted model. Keep the large model for the open-ended steps. Not checked first-hand: the practice page, read 2026-11-20 through a fetch summary, so re-check the wording on the page; see research/aiforscience.md.

title: Three Kinds of Machine
text:
Generative or predictive?
You will also hear models split into generative AI and predictive AI. The split cuts across the three kinds above. IBM’s explainer puts it this way:

Predictive AI finds patterns in past data to forecast what is likely to happen next: a sales figure, a fraud flag, a demand estimate. It is usually trained on a smaller, targeted dataset for one question, and its numbers are easier to explain.
Generative AI produces new content (text, code, images, audio) that resembles its training data without copying it. It is trained on very large datasets, and it is usually much harder to explain why it gave a particular answer.

Both predict in a loose sense: an LLM predicts the next word. The difference is what you want out. Predictive AI gives you an estimate to act on, and generative AI gives you new material to review.
In this quest’s terms, a trained model (a classifier, a gene-finder, a structure predictor) mostly sits on the predictive side, and an LLM is the usual example of generative AI. The line is not clean. A generative model can be asked to classify, as in the label-tidying example above, and some generative models predict structure or sequences. Judge the tool by the task you give it and how you will check the result.
IBM also makes a practical point: a task that needs a forecast usually does not need a generative model, because a simpler predictive model does it more cheaply. That is the same advice as picking the simplest machine that does the job.
Source: IBM Think, “Generative AI vs. predictive AI: What’s the difference?”, published 2024-08-09, read 2026-11-20. A vendor explainer. The mapping onto the three kinds is this course’s own.

title: Three Kinds of Machine
section: Should you fine-tune? A note on LoRA
text:
Should you fine-tune? A note on LoRA
You may meet LoRA (low-rank adaptation) and wonder if it is the next step. It is a way to fine-tune: you freeze the model’s weights and train small extra “adapter” matrices on your own examples. That needs far less memory than retraining everything, and the adapter can later be merged into the base model. It changes the model itself, so it belongs to the trained model kind above, not to the way you prompt an LLM.
LoRA tends to be worth considering only when all of these hold:

You have the model weights. An open-weight model you can download qualifies. A hosted model you reach through an API usually does not (a few providers offer their own fine-tuning service, which is a different route).
The task is narrow and repeatable: the same kind of input and the same kind of output every time, such as masking one class of identifier or tagging text with a fixed label set.
You have labelled examples, enough to train on and to hold some back for testing.
You have an eval that shows the tuned model beats the untuned one on that task. Without one, you cannot tell whether training helped.

For agent work, a clearer prompt, better tools and a working eval usually give more return first, and they cost less to change. Try those, and fine-tune only when you can show they fall short on a narrow task. Fine-tuning also adds new things to track: the training data, the adapter version and the base model it belongs to.
If you do want to follow up, the two links in the Lore below are runnable starting points. One is a beginner guide from a tooling vendor, and the other is the library documentation behind most LoRA code.
General practice, not a vendor claim. Not run by this course. What LoRA does is from the Hugging Face PEFT docs and Unsloth guide, read 2026-11-20. Sources: research/lore-extra.md

What a model can do on its own
It helps to remember what a language model does well with no tools at all. Apple’s developer guide for its small on-device model lists this plainly, and the list is a good reminder for any model on its own (the guide is about a small model, so a large hosted model will do better on some rows):







A model on its own tends to suit
A model on its own tends to struggle with




Summarising and editing text
Counting letters or doing basic arithmetic


Pulling out names, places and other entities
Writing code (for that model)


Classifying or judging a piece of text
Multi-step logical reasoning


Generating tags, or short creative writing
Facts it was never given



Apple’s page says harder tasks become possible once the model can call tools or produce structured output. That is the idea behind an agent: the model reads and writes, and a harness gives it tools (a shell, a file editor, a script runner) for the parts it finds hard. Counting and arithmetic are good examples of work to hand to a script.

This page makes no claim that using an LLM agent on a cluster is allowed or expected. Many sites have rules, and some forbid it for certain data. Ask your cluster staff. This quest is reading only. title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
What lives where
Claude Code keeps sessions, settings and plugins in ~/.claude, and writes ~/.claude.json (account details, MCP configuration, trust decisions). CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR relocates the first of these.
General practice: if your home directory is shared across nodes, then session history, which can contain pasted data or paths, sits on shared storage. Check who can read it (for example chmod 700 ~/.claude) and whether home is backed up or group-readable. The docs do not say this; it is an inference.
Settings files, from the docs: user ~/.claude/settings.json, project .claude/settings.json (commit it), local .claude/settings.local.json, and managed settings. Precedence is managed, then command line, then local, then shared project, then user. Permission lists merge across files. An organisation can enforce managed settings that your own files cannot override, so your site may already have decided some of this.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Keys

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, when set, overrides a subscription login. In -p (non-interactive) mode it is always used, and interactive mode asks you once to approve it. If a key is exported in a shared profile, the key in use may not be the one you expect.
General practice: never put a key in a script or in a committed .claude/settings.json. On a shared account, use a per-user key kept in a file readable only by you (mode 600), and do not keep a lab-wide key in a shared directory.
The sandbox’s default reads cover most of the machine, including credential files such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials. Use Read(...) deny rules or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead for key files. Remember that the sandbox covers shell commands only.

Not confirmed here: how OpenCode stores keys, and what the apiKeyHelper setting does. Check the docs for your version.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Data and egress
Egress means data leaving the machine.

General practice: before any cluster data, paths, logs or code go to an external model API, check your institution’s policy. Human genomic, clinical or controlled-access data often has agreements that forbid third-party processing.
Read is auto-approved inside the working directory. A project folder holding controlled data is therefore readable by the agent unless a Read(...) deny rule or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead covers it. General practice: keep controlled data outside the agent’s working directory and give the agent synthetic or de-identified test data.
General practice, not checked in the docs, so ask your site: some sites restrict internet access from compute nodes, so an agent there may not reach a model API at all. A common pattern is the agent on your laptop, writing scripts, with jobs running offline. Some sites forbid agents on login nodes and allow them only in an interactive compute allocation, where internet access may be restricted. Ask staff which applies. A plain ssh from inside the Claude Code sandbox does not work as a hop.
The sandbox’s network.allowedDomains starts empty, so unlisted hosts prompt (in the default modes).


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


If your project has an instruction file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) stricter than a generic skill, the stricter one wins, and your cluster’s policy outranks both. The same questions apply. Not checked here: whether a local model through Ollama changes what your data agreement requires, so ask.
