title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Prerequisites: RAG and Its Cousins, and Adopt the Pet (Ollama installed and running). Python 3 on your path; the scripts use only its standard library. This is an optional side quest. Objective: build a small knowledge graph from twelve mock lab notes using a local model, query it, compare it with simple RAG, and know what it takes to use LightRAG or Microsoft GraphRAG with Ollama. Time: about 30 minutes, most of it waiting for the model. Everything stays on your machine, and the notes are mock data.
Verified: ran rag.py and graph.py on 2026-11-20 (macOS, Ollama 0.40.16) with gemma4:12b-mlx for chat and nomic-embed-text for embeddings. One run per question at temperature 0, not repeated. A second run on 2026-11-20 used Mistral’s ministral-3:8b for chat (same embeddings, see “A second model”). Not run: LightRAG, Microsoft GraphRAG, qwen3:4b. Tool facts for those two: Last verified (docs, not run) on 2026-11-20. Sources: research/rag.md.
Files: mini-rag holds ollama_min.py (two helpers), rag.py (simple RAG), graph.py (a hand-made graph RAG) and notes/ (twelve short mock notes, 233 words in all). Save the folder anywhere. If the link is not available, ask your agent to recreate it from the descriptions below.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Set up
Pull an embedding model and pick a chat model you already have. Adopt the Pet suggested qwen3:4b, which this quest did not test (a small model may extract worse facts; see the model note below).
ollama pull nomic-embed-text
export CHAT_MODEL=gemma4:12b-mlx      # or any chat model you have pulled
cd mini-rag
The scripts read three environment variables: CHAT_MODEL, EMBED_MODEL (default nomic-embed-text) and OLLAMA_URL (default http://127.0.0.1:11434). They send each request with num_ctx set to 8192, so you do not have to restart the server for them; Adopt the Pet explains why the default context is small.
Open notes/ and read a few. They are fictional: two sequencers (Orion and Vega), two projects (Heron and Kelp), two pipeline releases, and some distractors such as the lunch rota. One of the questions we will ask needs a chain of four hops: Project Heron studies samples S31 to S36, run R7 loaded those samples, run R7 used pipeline release 2.3, and release 2.3 has a known bug.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 1: simple RAG
rag.py is the four steps from the last quest in about thirty lines: embed every note, embed the question, keep the k closest notes, ask the model to answer from them.
python3 rag.py "Does project Heron need to re-analyse its data because of a known pipeline bug?"
What we got with the default -k 3:
Retrieved:
  0.668  pipeline-2-4.txt
  0.653  pipeline-2-3.txt
  0.644  project-heron.txt

Answer:
The notes do not contain the answer.
The notes that hold the answer were in the folder, but the run log that connects Heron’s samples to pipeline 2.3 ranked fourth. Try -k 5:
  0.668  pipeline-2-4.txt
  0.653  pipeline-2-3.txt
  0.644  project-heron.txt
  0.549  run-r7.txt
  0.528  run-r8.txt

Answer:
Yes, project Heron needs to re-analyse its data because the primary analysis of run R7 used pipeline release 2.3, which has a known bug that double-counts duplicate reads.
And --all, which skips retrieval and pastes every note into the prompt, also gave a correct answer. With twelve short notes, the window holds everything, which is the “small collection” row of the table in the last quest.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 2: build the graph
graph.py build sends each note to the chat model and asks for (subject, relation, object) facts. It uses Ollama’s structured outputs: the request carries a JSON schema in the format field, so the reply is JSON in the shape the script expects. Ollama’s docs suggest temperature 0 for this, and the helper sets it.
python3 graph.py build
python3 graph.py show
In our run it printed saved 67 facts, and the whole build took 1 minute 20 seconds for twelve notes. A sample of what show printed:
Run R7 --loaded onto--> Orion    [run-r7.txt]
Run R7 --used--> Pipeline 2.3    [run-r7.txt]
Pipeline 2.3 --has bug--> double-counts duplicate reads    [pipeline-2-3.txt]
Project Heron --studies--> S31    [project-heron.txt]
Orion --looked after by--> Dana Okafor    [orion.txt]
You --bring--> own cup    [lunch.txt]
Read the whole list. Most facts match their notes. Two did not: the lunch note produced You --bring--> own cup, which is not a fact about anything in the lab, and one name came back with a stray leading space, which would have split a single entity into two nodes (the script now strips names when it loads them). Extraction is a model’s reading of your text, so a graph is a second thing to check. Every fact carries the note it came from, so you can.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 3: ask the graph
graph.py ask does three things. It finds starting entities (names that appear in the question, plus the three closest by embedding). It walks outward two hops along the links. Then it hands the collected facts and their source notes to the model.
python3 graph.py ask "Does project Heron need to re-analyse its data because of a known pipeline bug?"
Starting entities: ['pipeline 2.3', 'pipeline 2.4', 'project heron']
Collected 40 facts from 8 notes: freezers.txt, meeting-march.txt, pipeline-2-3.txt, pipeline-2-4.txt, project-heron.txt, project-kelp.txt, run-r7.txt, run-r8.txt

Answer:
Yes, Project Heron needs to re-analyse its data because Run R7, which loaded the samples for Project Heron (S31 to S36), used Pipeline 2.3, which has a known bug that double-counts duplicate reads.

Notes used:
- [pipeline-2-3.txt]
- [project-heron.txt]
- [run-r7.txt]
The wording of the answer differs a little from run to run even at temperature 0 (we saw two versions), so yours will not match word for word.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
section: What this shows, and what it does not
text:
What this shows, and what it does not

Simple RAG missed at k=3 and succeeded at k=5. The failure was a retrieval miss: the run log was not among the top three notes. Raising k fixed it here, at the price of more text in the prompt.
Putting everything in the prompt also worked, because the collection is tiny.
The graph walk reached the run log without a bigger k, because the link from Heron’s samples to run R7 is an edge. It also pulled in 40 of the 67 facts and 8 of the 12 notes, so the walk is broad, and a bigger collection would need a smaller hop count or a ranking step.
The graph cost a minute and twenty seconds to build for 233 words, and it needs a model good enough to extract facts. Embedding twelve notes for simple RAG takes seconds. General practice: the build cost grows with the size of the collection, and Microsoft’s paper reports hours for a roughly 1-million-token corpus.
This is one question, one model and one run. It illustrates the mechanics and proves nothing about which method is better. Try your own questions.
A whole-collection question failed in all three setups. We asked “Who works in this group, and what does each person do?” and simple RAG, --all and the graph walk each said the notes did not contain the answer. No note lists a roster, so it may simply be a poor question. Microsoft’s Graph RAG aims at whole-collection questions with community summaries; this toy graph does not build any.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
A second model: Mistral’s Ministral 3
Models behave differently on the same notes, and swapping one is a one-line change (export CHAT_MODEL=...). We repeated the runs with ministral-3:8b from Mistral. Ollama lists it at 6.0 GB with tool support and an Apache 2.0 licence (Last verified, docs, not run, on 2026-11-20; see research/mistral.md). For simple RAG, retrieval did not change, since the embedding model is the same, so the same notes came back at each k. Only the answering model differed. The graph was rebuilt by the new model, so its walk differs (25 facts from 7 notes, against 40 facts from 8 notes with gemma4:12b-mlx). One run per question at temperature 0:








Setup
gemma4:12b-mlx
ministral-3:8b




Simple RAG, -k 3
“The notes do not contain the answer.”
Says the notes do not contain enough information.


Simple RAG, -k 5
Yes, re-analysis needed (correct).
No (wrong): it claims run R7 used release 2.4, but the note says 2.3.


--all (every note pasted)
Correct.
Lists the right facts (R7 used 2.3, which has the bug), then answers No because “no re-analysis was done” (wrong).


Graph walk
Yes (correct).
Collects 25 facts from 7 notes, including the R7 and 2.3 facts, then answers No (wrong).


Whole-collection question
Not answered.
Not answered.



The graph build with ministral-3:8b took about a minute, saved 80 facts and returned valid JSON for all twelve notes. Reading show turned up a few odd entries: Pipeline 2.3 --has issue fix--> Dana Okafor, a node called Pipeline 2.3 issue, and a User node taken from the safety note. We did not compare all 80 facts with their notes, so read show against the notes yourself.
What we take from it. With this model, the right passages reached the prompt in three setups (for the graph, passages from a graph this model built) and the final answer was still wrong, once with a misread (2.4 for 2.3) and twice with a reasoning slip. Retrieval is one half of the job, and the reader model is the other half. The check you can always do is the one this quest keeps asking for: read the notes it names and see whether they say what the answer says. General practice: test a model on a few questions whose answers you know before you trust it on new ones. This is one question, one run and two models, so it does not rank them. Mistral also offers mistral-small (24B, 14 GB) and others on Ollama, and we did not run those.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
A note on model size
Extraction asks a model to produce well-formed JSON for every chunk. The tools’ own documentation is cautious about small models: the Microsoft GraphRAG docs say that with Ollama they “frequently see issues with malformed responses (especially JSON)”, and the LightRAG README calls a 30B-parameter model “a reasonable minimum” for local use, while its programming guide says at least 32B. Neither gives a benchmark. Our 12B model produced valid JSON for all twelve notes, and show lets you judge the facts. Not checked: how qwen3:4b or other models under about 7B do on this exercise. If you try one, read the triples before you trust the answers.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
section: Using a real tool with Ollama
text:
Using a real tool with Ollama
graph.py is a teaching toy. Two real projects do this at scale. Treat the details below as Last verified (docs, not run), and check the current docs before relying on them.
LightRAG (github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG; release v1.5.8rc1 on 2026-11-15 when read).

Install: pip install "lightrag-hku[api]" (the README also shows uv), then copy env.example to .env and run lightrag-server.
For Ollama, the project’s guide wires ollama_model_complete for chat and ollama_embed for embeddings. Its docs say LightRAG “requires at least 32k context tokens” and that Ollama’s default is smaller. Set num_ctx to 32768 in code or in a Modelfile; for the server, OLLAMA_LLM_NUM_CTX in .env. Ollama’s own docs say the default context is 4k on machines under 24 GiB of video memory, so check with ollama ps.
Use a non-thinking model for extraction. The README says models slower than about 50 tokens per second may time out on dense chunks.
Pick your embedding model before indexing and keep it. EMBEDDING_DIM must equal the model’s output size. The guide uses 768 for nomic-embed-text. Changing the model later means re-embedding everything.
The default storage is in-memory files meant for small tests.
Server safety: the docs say lightrag-server binds to all network interfaces with authentication off by default. On a laptop or shared machine, set HOST=127.0.0.1 before you start it.

Microsoft GraphRAG (microsoft.github.io/graphrag; v3.3.0 on 2026-10-08 when read).

The commands are graphrag init, graphrag index and graphrag query "..." --method local (or global). Text files go in input/.
The docs warn that it “can consume a lot of LLM resources” and suggest starting with the small tutorial dataset and cheaper models.
It calls models through LiteLLM and requires structured JSON output. The docs describe users putting Ollama behind a proxy and report frequent malformed responses. Not checked: a documented Ollama setup (none was found in the docs). A closed GitHub issue reports that its default embedding vector size of 3072 can clash with smaller embedding models such as the 768-dimension nomic-embed-text, which is issue evidence, not official guidance.

General practice: if you want a graph over your own notes with Ollama, start with LightRAG on a tiny folder of mock files, then look at the facts it extracted before pointing it at anything real.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Verify the graph
The Blight likes a confident answer built on a wrong link. A graph gives you something to check that a plain answer does not: the list of facts, each with its source note.

Read the extracted facts for a few notes against the notes themselves. Count the wrong ones.
Ask the agent or the script to name the notes behind each answer, then open them.
Keep a short list of questions whose answers you know, and run it after you change the model, the prompt or the notes.
Never put real or controlled data in this exercise. The same scripts pointed at a hosted model would send every note to that provider; see The Locked Cabinet.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
Prerequisites: RAG and Its Cousins. This is an optional side quest. Objective: explain what an LLM-maintained wiki is and why someone would keep one, describe its three layers and three jobs, match it to a use case from your own work, and know where it can go wrong, including how it sits on top of an Obsidian vault. Time: about 25 minutes. Reading and planning only; you choose whether to build anything afterwards.
Last verified (docs, not run): the “LLM Wiki” gist by Andrej Karpathy (created 2026-04-04), read in full on 2026-11-20. Not run: building a wiki, Obsidian, qmd. Claims about Obsidian beyond what the gist says are marked General practice. Sources: research/llm-wiki.md.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
The itch
Think about the last time you read ten papers on a method, or went through six months of meeting notes. You understood it all at the time. A month later, the understanding lives in your head and in a pile of files, and the next question sends you back to the pile.
RAG answers that with a lookup: each question searches the pile again, pastes a few passages into the prompt, and starts from scratch. Nothing builds up between questions. If an answer needs five documents stitched together, the stitching is redone every time.
The gist this quest is based on proposes another arrangement. Let an agent keep a wiki: a folder of interlinked Markdown pages that it writes and updates as new sources arrive, so the stitching is done once and stays. The gist’s own words for it: a “persistent, compounding artifact”. Its argument is that people drop their notes because the bookkeeping is tedious (updating links, rewriting summaries, spotting that two pages now disagree), and that bookkeeping is exactly what an agent does without getting bored. You keep the parts that need a person: choosing sources, asking questions, and deciding what the findings mean.
The author calls the file an “idea file”, meant to be handed to your agent so the two of you work out the details together. It describes a pattern, and it does not include a program or any measurements. Everything below is that pattern plus our own cautions.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
Three layers



Layer
Who writes it
What it holds




Raw sources
You add files; nobody edits them afterwards.
Papers, clipped web pages, meeting transcripts, run logs, data files. The gist calls them immutable: the agent reads them and never changes them. They are the source of truth.


The wiki
The agent. You read it.
Markdown pages: a summary per source, a page per entity (a tool, a dataset, a person, a gene) or concept, comparisons, an overview. The agent owns this folder.


The schema
You and the agent, over time.
One instruction file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, AGENTS.md in OpenCode) describing how the wiki is organised and what to do on each job. The gist calls it the key configuration file. See The Project Charter for how these files work.



The split matters for trust. When an answer looks odd, you can walk from the wiki page back to the raw source it cites, and the raw source has not been touched.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
Three jobs
Ingest. You drop one source into the raw folder and ask the agent to process it. A typical pass: read the source, tell you the main takeaways, write a summary page, update the pages for the entities and concepts it mentions, add it to the index, and append a line to the log. The gist says one source may touch 10 to 15 pages. The author prefers to ingest one source at a time and stay involved, and mentions that batching with less supervision is possible.
Query. You ask a question. The agent finds the relevant wiki pages, reads them and answers with citations. The part that makes the wiki grow: a good answer (a comparison table, a timeline, a short report) is filed back as a new page, so your explorations add to the wiki and do not vanish into chat history.
Lint. From time to time you ask for a health check. The gist lists what to look for: pages that contradict each other, claims that a newer source has overtaken, pages that nothing links to, concepts that are mentioned but have no page, missing cross-references, and gaps that a web search might fill.
Two small files keep it navigable:

index.md is a catalogue: each page with a link and a one-line summary, grouped by category, updated on every ingest. To answer a question, the agent reads the index first and then opens the pages that look relevant. The gist says this works well at moderate scale (about 100 sources and a few hundred pages) and avoids building an embedding index. That is the author’s experience; we did not test it.
log.md is an append-only diary of ingests, queries and lint passes. The gist suggests giving every entry the same prefix so a simple grep can list the recent ones.

General practice for your own first version, as an example schema you could paste into the instruction file and then edit with your agent. It was not run:
# Wiki rules
- `raw/` holds sources. Never edit or delete anything in `raw/`.
- `wiki/` holds pages you write. One page per entity or concept; one summary page per source in `wiki/sources/`.
- Every claim on a wiki page ends with a link to the source file it came from. If no source supports it, mark it `(unsourced)`.
- On ingest: read the source, tell me the three main takeaways and wait for my reply, then write the summary page, update affected pages, update `wiki/index.md`, and append `## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | <title>` to `wiki/log.md`.
- On lint: list contradictions, unsourced claims, orphan pages and missing pages. Do not fix anything until I say which.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
section: Why you might want this, and what it costs
text:
Why you might want this, and what it costs



Approach
Where it helps
What you pay




Paste everything into the prompt
Small collections (see the table in RAG and Its Cousins). No setup.
Repeated reading each session; a limit at the window size.


RAG
A large, changing pile; questions answered by particular passages.
Each question starts from scratch; multi-document answers are re-stitched; retrieval misses are silent (see RAG and Its Cousins).


A wiki the agent maintains
Material you will return to for weeks or months, where understanding should accumulate and be readable.
Agent time and tokens on every ingest (several pages touched per source); a layer of text that can contain mistakes; your review time.


Notes you write yourself
Things you want to think through in your own words. A perfectly good choice; the wiki pays off when the bookkeeping is what stops you.
The bookkeeping, which is the part people tend to drop.



The wiki and RAG can also sit together: the gist suggests adding a search tool to the wiki once the index alone is not enough, and names qmd (a local Markdown search tool; Not checked: we have not read or run it). General practice: a wiki is a good home for the stable understanding, and RAG or search is a good way to reach the raw sources behind it.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
Use cases you may recognise
The gist lists personal, research, reading a book, team, and “competitive analysis, due diligence, trip planning, course notes, hobby deep-dives”. Here are some closer to a bioinformatics desk. They are our examples, not from the gist, and none was run.










Use case
Raw sources
Pages the agent might keep
A question it could answer
Watch out for




Literature on one method (say, long-read assemblers or variant callers)
Papers, preprints, tool docs
One page per tool and per dataset; a comparison table; a page of open disagreements between papers
“Which papers compare tool A and B on the same data, and do they agree?”
Preprints and abstracts mixed with peer-reviewed papers. Ask the agent to record the kind of source on every page.


The lab’s pipeline handbook
Release notes, run logs, meeting minutes, Slack exports
One page per pipeline release, one per known issue, a decision log (“why we changed the aligner settings”)
“Which runs used release 2.3, and what was wrong with it?”
Private or unpublished material (see the risks below). Exact counts belong to a query tool, not a wiki page.


A thesis or long project
Papers you read, your own notes on experiments, supervisor meeting notes
A running thesis page, an open-questions page, one page per experiment
“What did I conclude about batch effects in March, and what has changed since?”
A wiki that you never read. You will not remember what you did not read, even if the wiki does.


A course, a workshop or onboarding
Slides, lecture notes, tutorials, the docs for your tools
Glossary, one page per concept, a “things that confused me” page
“Explain the difference between X and Y using only what the course covered.”
Source material goes stale quickly for fast-moving tools. Date every source.


Reference notes for the tools you use
Docs pages, GitHub issues, your own gotchas
One page per tool with versions, quirks and a link to the source
“What did we learn the last time this tool ran out of memory?”
Version drift. Record the version on each page and re-check on upgrade.


A book or a long series
Chapters, episode notes
Characters, themes, a timeline, built up as you read
“Where did this thread first appear?”
Spoilers for yourself. Ingest as you read.



To size your own idea, answer four questions in a sentence each: What sources would go in? How often do they change? What question would I ask in a month that I cannot answer quickly today? Who may read these sources, and where may they be sent? If the sources fit in one prompt, try that first. If the question is an exact filter or count, ask a query tool. If the sources are sensitive and you would send them to a hosted model, read The Locked Cabinet before you begin. If the material is something you want to return to and the answers need several sources joined, the wiki is a good candidate.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
Where Obsidian fits
If you already use Obsidian, you have most of what the pattern needs. General practice (Obsidian’s own docs were not read for this page): an Obsidian vault is a folder of Markdown files, so an agent can read and write it like any other folder, and Obsidian shows whatever is there. The gist describes working with the agent on one side and Obsidian open on the other, with the line “Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase.” You read, and the agent edits.
A layout that follows the three layers:
my-vault/
  raw/            sources you add (clippings, PDFs, transcripts); the agent never edits these
    assets/       downloaded images
  wiki/           pages the agent writes
    index.md
    log.md
    sources/  entities/  concepts/
  CLAUDE.md       the schema (or AGENTS.md)
What the gist names for Obsidian (the one-line descriptions of each tool are General practice; Obsidian’s docs were not read):

Web Clipper, a browser extension that turns a web article into a Markdown file, so a source can land in raw/ in one click.
Graph view, to see the shape of the wiki: hubs, and orphan pages that nothing links to. The gist calls it a good way to see the shape of the wiki, and it doubles as a quick visual check.
Dataview, a plugin that queries the properties at the top of each page. If your schema asks the agent to add them (a source type, a date, a version), you get live tables, such as every page whose status is unsourced.
Marp, a Markdown slide format with an Obsidian plugin, for turning an answer into slides.
Images: the gist suggests fixing the attachment folder (for example raw/assets/) and binding a hotkey that downloads a clipped page’s images locally. It also notes that an agent cannot read a Markdown file with inline images in a single pass and should read the text first and look at the images afterwards. The author calls this clunky.

Habits we suggest, all General practice:

Keep the agent’s folder separate from the notes you write by hand. Your own words stay yours, and you can tell at a glance what the agent produced.
Put the vault under git and commit before each ingest. The gist points out that the wiki is just a git repository of Markdown files. A commit per ingest gives you a readable diff of what the agent changed and an undo; see The Shield of Undo.
Make raw/ read-only if your tools allow it, so that the rule “never edit raw” is enforced by the system as well as written in the instruction file. The instruction file only advises (Advice or Enforcement).
If you do not use Obsidian, any editor that opens a folder of Markdown files works. The pattern does not depend on it.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
What can go wrong

A mistake becomes a fact. If the agent misreads a source, the error lands on a page, and later pages cite that page. The cost grows with each ingest. General practice: require a source link on every claim, skim the diff of every ingest, and use lint to hunt for unsourced claims. One source at a time, as the author suggests, makes the skimming practical.
The agent edits what it should only read. Keep sources immutable, as the gist says, and check it with git.
Clipped pages can carry instructions. A web page you clip may contain text aimed at your agent, and the agent reads it during ingest and then writes files. OWASP’s warning about retrieved text, covered in RAG and Its Cousins, applies, and Guard the Door shows how to limit what the agent may do. Review the diff, and keep an agent with write access away from sources you do not trust.
Sources leave your machine. With a hosted model, every source you ingest is sent as prompt text. For unpublished results, patient-linked data or anything under an agreement, check the rules first (The Locked Cabinet). Running a local model through Ollama keeps text on your machine, but small models find ingest hard: it asks for reading, summarising and editing several files in one go. Not checked: how well small local models do this. Try one short, harmless source first.
Cost and time grow with the wiki. Each ingest reads the index and several pages, and then writes several. General practice: watch your usage in the first week (Memory, Sessions and Usage).
Scale. The index approach is described for roughly a hundred sources. Beyond that, expect to add search or another layer. Not checked by us.
You may not learn it. A wiki you never open does little for your own understanding. Treat it as something you read, correct and argue with. Name the Fears has a worry about hollow accomplishment, and this is a place where it applies.
Exact answers. Counts, filters and joins over tables belong in a query tool, not in prose pages, for the reason given in RAG and Its Cousins.

text:
With a companion

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Put the schema in CLAUDE.md at the root of the wiki folder. Start a session there, and ask the agent to read the schema and propose the folder layout before it writes anything. Use Plan before you edit for the first ingest, then tighten the schema with whatever you correct. Keep ingest, query and lint as separate short sessions (When to Start Fresh), since the wiki itself is the memory that carries over.


Put the schema in AGENTS.md at the root of the wiki folder (OpenCode also falls back to CLAUDE.md). With a local model, start with a handful of short, non-sensitive sources and check each page against its source, because a small model is more likely to drop or garble details. If a model struggles with the multi-file edit, ask it to do the ingest in steps: summary page first, then one entity page at a time.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Prerequisites: The Context Window. This is an optional side quest. Objective: explain what retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is, tell apart simple RAG, improved RAG, Graph RAG, LightRAG and the loop-style variants, and choose between RAG and the other ways of answering questions from a pile of documents. Time: about 20 minutes. Reading only; the hands-on follow-up is Grow a Graph with Ollama.
Last verified (docs, not run): the papers, docs and posts listed in Lore, read on 2026-11-20. Sources: research/rag.md. Numbers are the authors’ own unless the text says otherwise.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Why anyone brings RAG up
A model knows what it learned in training. It has not read your lab’s protocols, last month’s run logs or the paper that came out last week. You can paste documents into the prompt, but the window (the text the model can see at once; see The Context Window) is finite, and a long prompt costs money and time.
RAG is the idea of looking things up first. A program searches your documents for the passages most likely to matter, pastes only those into the prompt, and asks the model to answer from them. The name comes from a 2020 paper by Lewis and colleagues, which paired a generator with a vector index of Wikipedia. The recipe most people mean today is a later, simpler version of that idea.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Simple RAG in four steps

Chunk. Split the documents into pieces (a chunk is one passage, often a paragraph or a few hundred words).
Embed. An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector (a long list of numbers; texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions). The vectors are stored in an index.
Retrieve. Embed the question the same way, then fetch the k chunks whose vectors are closest (k is a number you pick, such as 3 or 5).
Generate. Paste those chunks into the prompt and ask the model to answer from them and to say which chunk it used.

Step 1 has its own pitfalls. Papers and PDFs hold tables, figures and two-column text, and a plain text extractor can scramble them before anything is embedded. A community notebook collection describes a results table losing its structure this way (we did not run it). General practice: open a few extracted chunks and read them before you trust the index.
Everything the model says is limited by step 3. If the right passage did not come back, the model cannot use it, and a good model will either say it does not know or, worse, answer from the wrong passages.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
A tour of the types
Names overlap and new ones appear every month. Think of them as answers to the question: what goes wrong with simple RAG, and what did someone add to fix it?









Type
What it adds
Good for
Watch out for




Simple RAG
Chunk, embed, top-k, answer.
A pile of prose where each question is answered by one or two passages. Cheap to build and to update.
Questions that need several passages, or the whole collection, since only the top k chunks arrive.


Improved RAG
Add-ons around the same pipeline: keyword search (BM25, a classic word-matching score) next to embeddings, a reranker (a second model that re-sorts the retrieved chunks), a short context line added to each chunk before embedding, and rewriting the question or drafting a made-up answer first (HyDE) to search with.
Raising the chance the right chunk comes back. Anthropic reports that adding context, BM25 and a reranker cut its top-20 retrieval failures from 5.7% to 1.9% on its own tests.
Each add-on is another moving part to tune. HyDE’s own paper says the drafted answer “is unreal and may contain false details”.


Graph RAG (Microsoft)
Before any question, an LLM reads every chunk and extracts entities and relationships into a knowledge graph (things as nodes, links between them as edges). It groups the graph into communities and writes a summary of each.
Questions about the whole collection, such as “what are the main themes?”, answered from community summaries.
Indexing is slow and costly: the paper reports 281 minutes for a roughly 1-million-token corpus with GPT-4 Turbo. The docs warn that it “can consume a lot of LLM resources”.


LightRAG
Also builds an entity graph with an LLM, but skips the communities. A query is turned into keywords, matched against entities and relations, and the neighbours are added. New documents merge into the graph without a rebuild.
A lighter graph approach that updates incrementally, with modes from plain chunks (naive) to graph-based (local, global, hybrid, mix).
The project says it needs a stronger model than plain RAG: its README calls a 30B-parameter model “a reasonable minimum” for local use.


Tree RAG (RAPTOR)
Clusters chunks and summarises them in layers, so a question can match a detail or a summary.
Long documents where the answer may be a broad theme.
Another build step with an LLM; tested mainly on question-answering benchmarks.


Loop-style RAG (Self-RAG, Corrective RAG, agentic RAG)
The system decides when to retrieve, checks what came back, tries again or searches the web. A survey groups these as “agentic RAG”.
Questions where one lookup is rarely enough.
More model calls per question. Self-RAG needs a model trained for it.



General practice: the “good for” column is our reading of what each method is built to do. The “watch out” figures come from the sources named in Lore.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Does the graph pay off?
The papers that introduced Graph RAG and LightRAG report wins over plain RAG. Those results are self-reported: an LLM judge compared answers on questions that another LLM generated, mostly about whole collections, and the authors of LightRAG note that ground truth is hard to define for such questions.
Independent studies give a more mixed picture:

A 2026 comparison (Han and colleagues) found “complementary behaviors rather than a consistent winner”. On single-fact questions from Natural Questions, plain RAG scored best (F1 64.78 against 63.01 for the best graph variant here). On multi-hop questions (an answer that needs facts from two or more passages) a graph method led by a few points. Building the graphs took far longer (135 seconds for plain RAG against 5,560 for one Graph RAG variant on the same corpus), and only about 65% of the answer entities ended up in the graphs.
The same study found that an LLM judge can flip its verdict when you swap the order of the two answers. Treat win-rate numbers as weak evidence.
A second study (Xiang and colleagues) concludes that graphs help when a task connects ideas across documents and can add noise on simple lookups.

General practice: start with simple RAG, measure it on questions you care about, and add a graph only if the failures are of the kind a graph addresses (multi-hop or whole-collection questions) and you can afford the extra cost.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
section: When RAG is the right tool
text:
When RAG is the right tool
RAG is one of several ways to get a model to work from your documents. Here is how to choose.








Your situation
Often a better fit
Why




The whole collection is small (under about 200,000 tokens, roughly 500 pages)
Put it all in the prompt.
Anthropic’s post says that below that size you can include everything with no need for RAG. Prompt caching (reusing an unchanged prompt prefix at a lower price) makes repeated questions cheaper. Check the current pricing and cache lifetime.


The same large documents are asked about again and again
Long context with caching, or cache-augmented generation (preload everything once).
One paper found it faster than RAG on small question-answering sets, and its authors say it “becomes impractical for significantly larger datasets”.


Files you can search by name or exact text (code, configs, scripts)
Let an agent use search tools such as glob and grep.
Anthropic describes Claude Code navigating “just-in-time” with these, and says exploring at run time is slower than reading a pre-built index.


Tables and databases (“all samples deeper than 30x in liver tissue”, counts, joins)
A query tool: SQL, an API or an MCP server.
General practice (no source opened): a vector index returns the nearest passages, so it cannot promise a complete filter or an exact count. A query can, and you can read the query.


Exact words matter (gene names, sample ids, error codes)
Keyword search first, or hybrid.
BM25 is a strong baseline in the BEIR benchmark, and adding it to embeddings cut Anthropic’s retrieval failures further.


You want the model to follow a format or style
Better prompts, a Skill, or fine-tuning.
OpenAI’s guide says to fine-tune when the problem is consistency or behaviour, and to supply context when the model lacks knowledge. Two papers found fine-tuning a poor way to add new facts. They did not test LoRA, so that is an inference.


A large, changing collection of prose, and questions answered by particular passages
RAG.
This is the case it was made for: the collection does not fit in the window, and you can update the index without retraining anything.



A study from Google researchers found that, with enough budget, a long-context model beat RAG on average, while RAG cost much less and gave the same answer on over 60% of queries. Their “Self-Route” idea tries RAG first and falls back to the long prompt, which cut cost by 39 to 65% on two models. These were 2024 models.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
section: What can go wrong with RAG itself
text:
What can go wrong with RAG itself

The right passage never comes back. Retrieval misses are normal. Measure them separately from the model’s answer: did the right chunk appear? and was the answer supported by the chunks it was given? The Ragas paper defines the second one as faithfulness. Splitting the two checks is our suggestion.
Too much arrives. More chunks can distract the model, and models use text in the middle of a long prompt less well than text at the start or end (see The Context Window and the “Lost in the Middle” paper in Lore).
Retrieved text can carry instructions. A document someone else wrote may contain lines aimed at your model. OWASP says RAG does not fully remove this risk. See Guard the Door for habits that limit the damage.
Chunks leave your machine. With a hosted model, retrieved passages are sent to the provider as ordinary prompt text. Whether that is allowed for your data is decided by your agreement; see The Locked Cabinet.
The index goes stale. Anything you indexed last month does not know about today’s edits until you rebuild it. General practice.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
With a companion

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Claude Code finds things in a project with its search tools rather than with a vector index you maintain; Anthropic’s engineering post names glob and grep. The Claude Code docs read for this page list a search tool category but do not explain why there is no index, so this page makes no claim about the reason. If you want RAG over your own papers, you build it yourself or connect a tool for it (see Plug In a Server), and then everything in the risks list above applies.


With Ollama you can run both halves locally: an embedding model for retrieval and a chat model for the answer. The next quest does this with a few short scripts. Not checked: how OpenCode itself searches a project.

text:
Honour

Think of one question you ask about your own work (a protocol, a sample sheet, a results table). Write one sentence saying which row of the “When RAG is the right tool” table fits it best, and why.


Estimate whether your own collection of notes would fit in a 200,000-token window. A rough rule is that one token is about three quarters of an English word, so 150,000 words is about 200,000 tokens. Ask your agent to count the words (wc -w) if you are unsure.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Prerequisites: When to Start Fresh. Objective: triage each new thought during a task into the right place (do now, park, quick question, helper, branch, or later session), and know what undo can and cannot restore. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): research/session-management.md sources on 2026-11-16 (Claude Code commands, sessions, worktrees, checkpointing and best-practices docs). Claude Code specific unless stated. Parking-lot files are general practice. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
Real work does not arrive in a straight line. You start fixing a samplesheet parser and think: “should I switch the aligner? What if I tried a stricter QC threshold? I also want to explore that other idea.” If you type every one of those into the same conversation, the context (everything the model can see when it writes its next reply, see The Context Window) fills with side tracks. Anthropic’s writing on context says accuracy and recall degrade as context grows, and the docs say the whole conversation is re-sent on every request, so a cluttered session tends to cost more per step (not checked: how much usage each route below saves; the research documents the mechanisms but gives no numbers). This is how a session ends up with three unrelated tasks that it “re-reads on every turn of the fourth”, in the docs’ words. A turn is one prompt from you plus the model’s reply.
Ideas are welcome. The fix is to triage each one.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Terms used here

Session: one saved conversation with the tool, tied to a project folder.
Subagent: a helper the main agent starts. It works in its own separate, clean context (it knows what you tell it) and sends back a summary, so its reading stays out of your conversation.
Conversation branch (/branch, which is separate from a git branch): a copy of the conversation from this point, so you can try something in the copy while the original stays as it was. /fork is a different command: it copies the conversation into a separate background session.
Git worktree: a second checkout of the same repository in another folder, so two sessions can edit files without overwriting each other.
Checkpoint: a snapshot Claude Code takes at each prompt you send, so you can roll back with /rewind.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
The triage
For each new thought, ask in this order. The key question is step 2: do you want the answer or the work during this session? If not, park it. If you do, steps 3 to 6 are the ways to get it.

Does it block the current task? Do it now, in this session.
Do you not want the answer or the work this session? Park it: write one line in a file and carry on (general practice, see below). Parked ideas leave through the “later session” exit: once the current task is done, pick from the file.
You want it now: is it a quick question you do not need on record? Use /btw <question>. It sees the conversation so far, has no tool access (it cannot read files, run commands or look at --help) and adds nothing to the history. So it suits questions about this conversation. An answer about a tool’s flags or defaults comes from the model’s memory: verify it against --help or the docs.
You want it now: is it exploration where you only need a summary? Ask for a subagent (it starts with its own clean context; the built-in Explore helper is a fast read-only searcher), or use /subtask <task>, which starts a background helper that inherits the whole conversation and returns its result here.
You want it now: is it a competing approach you want to try for real? Use /branch [name] to copy the conversation (the original stays reachable via /resume), or start a second session in its own worktree with claude --worktree <name>.
You want it now: is it a different task entirely? Finish the current one, commit your work, then /clear or start a new named session (claude -n <name>, or /rename <name> inside one).









New thought
Where it goes
Why




“The parser crashes on this sample ID” (it is the task)
Do now
It blocks you


“Maybe a stricter QC threshold would help”
Parking-lot line
You do not want the answer this session; no cost to the context


“Which sample did we exclude earlier?”
/btw
One answer from the conversation; no tools; stays out of the history


“Where is the aligner configured across the repo?”
Explore subagent or /subtask
Heavy reading stays out of your main context; you get a summary


“Try the other aligner and compare”
/branch or claude --worktree <name>
A real attempt that can fail without spoiling the main path


“Redo the plots for the other project” (you want to start it now)
Commit, then /clear or a new named session
Different task, different files, different context

title: The Stream of Ideas
section: What is and is not shared
text:
What is and is not shared
A worktree session isolates file edits only. Per the docs, claude --worktree <name> creates .claude/worktrees/<name>/ on a branch called worktree-<name>. Worktrees share the repository’s .git, and auto memory is per repository, so all worktrees share it. A fresh checkout does not contain gitignored files such as .env unless you list them in .worktreeinclude, and large data folders need worktree.symlinkDirectories or a setup step. Plan for that before you start a pipeline test in one.
/branch copies the conversation. Any background helpers still running keep reporting into the branch.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Checkpoints and /rewind
Every prompt you send is a checkpoint. /rewind (aliases /checkpoint, /undo; or press Esc twice on an empty prompt) lets you restore code and conversation, only the conversation, or only the code. The limits matter to bioinformatics: files changed only through Bash (the shell command tool) are not tracked, subagent edits are mostly not restored, and edits outside the session are not tracked. The docs say checkpoints are “not a replacement for version control”. A sed -i or a script that rewrites a results table is a Bash change (our inference from the limits), so exploring is safe only after you have committed.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
A parking-lot file
General practice (our inference, not a documented feature): no official page describes a parking-lot file. Keep it outside what the agent reads every session; the research cautions that a file imported into your instructions costs context each time. Keep it in the repository if the team should see it, in a gitignored file if it is personal, or use an issue tracker for anything that outlives the week.
# IDEAS.md  (one line each: date | idea | why it matters | revisit when)
2026-11-16 | Add a --dry-run flag to the parser | Check a samplesheet without writing output | after parser fix is merged
2026-11-16 | Stricter QC threshold (Q30 not Q20) | Fewer false variants in low-depth samples | when the test cohort is ready
2026-11-16 | Per-sample coverage plot | Spot dropouts faster | before the next batch

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Worked example
You are fixing a samplesheet parser that rejects sample IDs containing a dot.

“Does the pipeline require the dot at all?” That blocks the fix: do it now.
“Would a stricter QC threshold help?” You do not want the answer today: park it as a line in IDEAS.md.
“Which sample did we exclude earlier?” A quick question about this conversation: /btw. (Had it been “what does --min-qual default to?”, /btw could only guess from memory, so you would check --help instead.)
“Where else do we split sample IDs on dots?” Wide reading, only the list matters: Explore subagent.
“Let’s try the other aligner and compare.” A real experiment you want now: commit the fix, then /branch or a worktree session.
“I should also tidy the figures for the other project.” A different task you will start once the parser is done: later session: commit, /clear, or claude -n figures.

The main session ended with the parser fixed and a short, readable history.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands the docs confirm: /btw, /subtask, /branch, /fork, /rewind, /clear, /rename, /resume, claude -n <name>, claude --worktree <name> (or -w). Plan mode (/plan, or Shift+Tab until the bar shows it) makes Claude read and propose without editing until you approve. General practice (our inference): it suits a side idea you only want to think through.


Not checked: OpenCode’s side-question, branch and worktree features; the research could not find its share and fork pages. Documented on its terminal page: /new (alias /clear) for a fresh session, /sessions to return to one, /compact, and /undo and /redo (these need a git repository). General practice: a parking-lot file and a commit before exploring work in any tool, local models included.




Start a parking-lot file (or open an issue list) for your current project and add the three ideas on your mind, one line each with a reason and a trigger to revisit.


Look back at your last long session. Pick one side thought you followed and say where the triage would have sent it.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
Prerequisites: Who Said What. This is an optional side quest; Plug In a Server (advised) puts it to use. Objective: explain why a large toolset costs context and accuracy, and choose between a single call, a fixed workflow, an agent, and a plain script. Time: about 20 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude API tool-search docs, Claude Code MCP docs and Anthropic’s “Building effective agents” article on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/fundamentals.md). The figures quoted are Anthropic’s own claims and were not measured here. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
Every tool you give an agent has a definition: a name and a description of how to use it. The model needs those definitions in its window to choose a tool. That is the cost this quest is about, followed by the related question of whether you need an agent at all.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
Tools cost context
Anthropic’s tool-search docs say loading every tool definition up front causes context bloat. As an example they give a typical five-server setup that can use about 55 thousand tokens in definitions before any work starts. They also say Claude’s ability to pick the right tool degrades once you exceed 30 to 50 available tools. These are Anthropic’s statements on a docs page, with no method given, so read them as a rough guide to the shape of the problem; no thresholds were measured.
The same docs describe tool search: keep most definitions out of the window and load a few on demand. They say it typically cuts that overhead by over 85 percent, and they advise it from about 10 tools upward, or when definitions are large. Below that, plain tool calling is better.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Per the docs, MCP tool search is on by default: tool names and server instructions load at session start, and a full definition loads when needed (deferred). So extra MCP servers have a small effect on the window. It can be turned off with ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false, and on some older models it falls back to loading everything. Skills work the same way in spirit: descriptions load at start. /context shows what takes space. Whether the 30 to 50 tool accuracy claim still applies behind deferral is not stated in the docs we read. A community test (small, two runs, labelled preliminary) reported that turning a built-in tool off partway through a task discarded the cache and made the next turn cost about twenty times a normal one, while adding an MCP server did not. Choosing your tool set before you start avoids the question; the details are in When to Start Fresh.


Not checked: whether OpenCode defers tool definitions. Assume tool definitions cost context until you know otherwise, and keep the set small, especially on a local model with a small window (general practice).



The habit that follows (general practice, inferred from the above): few, clearly named tools, and remove the servers you do not use.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
section: Single call, workflow, agent, or script
text:
Single call, workflow, agent, or script
Anthropic’s article “Building effective agents” separates two things. A workflow orchestrates models and tools through paths fixed in code. An agent is a system where the model directs its own process and tool use. The article’s advice is to start with the simplest solution that works, and it says that building no agentic system (one where the model picks its own steps and tools) at all may be the right choice. For many uses, one well-prepared call is usually enough. It adds that agents trade speed and cost for performance, and that autonomy brings compounding errors, so test with limits: a stopping condition such as a maximum number of steps.
Our reading of that, as general practice:

A plain script when the rule is known. Counting reads, converting a format, running fastqc then trim then align in a fixed order. A Nextflow pipeline is already a workflow.
A single call when you paste the input and want a text answer, such as explaining an error.
An agent when the next step depends on what it finds, such as debugging a failing run or exploring an unfamiliar repository. Even then, give it a way to check its own work and a limit.

Using none of these is also a fine decision.
Does a team of agents help? One 2025 preprint from Google Research, Google DeepMind and MIT (“Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems”) compared a single agent with four multi-agent set-ups across 260 configurations on six benchmarks. Its findings, in short:

It depends on the task. On a task that splits into independent parts (financial analysis), multi-agent set-ups did far better than one agent, up to about 81 percent. On sequential planning, every multi-agent variant did worse, by 39 to 70 percent.
A strong single agent leaves little to gain. Once one agent already scored above about 45 percent on a task, adding agents gave diminishing or negative returns.
Unchecked agents pass errors on. Agents working independently amplified errors about 17 times, against about 4 times when a central agent checked the work.

Take-away (general practice): start with one agent, measure it, and add agents only for work that splits into independent parts and only if the measurement says it helps. The figures come from the authors’ own tasks and models and changed between versions of the preprint, so read them as direction, not as rules.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
Prerequisites: Tokens, Not Letters. Objective: sort jobs into “ask the model” and “run a script”, and name the other ways a model fails with one mitigation each. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): the sources listed in research/failure-modes.md (sections 6 and 7) on 2026-11-16. Verified: ran echo banana | grep -o n | wc -l and grep -c '>' on a three-record mock file. Items marked “general practice” or “Not checked:” are not from a source. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
A language model is good at some jobs and bad at others. The skill is knowing which is which before you trust the output. Using a model is always your choice. This quest shows where the risk sits if you do.

title: Where Machines Fail
section: Good jobs: the result is checkable
text:
Good jobs: the result is checkable
Models are generally useful where you can read the result, or run it, and judge it yourself (our inference from the research notes):

summarising text
drafting prose, such as a README or a methods first draft
explaining code or an error message
converting formats, for example a samplesheet CSV to JSON (a structured text format)
first drafts of code that you will then test

Caveat for summaries. A summary can leave things out or bend them. A peer-reviewed study of the older, pre-chat generation of summarisation models (Maynez et al., ACL 2020) found substantial unfaithful content in every system tested. That evidence is dated; the direction still applies. We found no published faithfulness rate for current Claude on scientific papers. So spot-check against the source: numbers, gene and sample names, direction of effect, negations. Omissions are harder to see, so skim the abstract and limitations yourself. Asking the model to quote the supporting lines first also helps; the Anthropic docs recommend quote-first extraction.

title: Where Machines Fail
section: Bad job: exact counting and arithmetic
text:
Bad job: exact counting and arithmetic
Ask a model: “How many n are in banana?” The right answer is 2 (b-a-n-a-n-a). A model can get this wrong, and can be wrong while sounding sure (see the overconfidence row below). A leading explanation is the one from the last quest: it reads tokens, which are chunks of letters (see Tokens, Not Letters). The state of the science is mixed. Some papers propose tokenisation as the cause (arXiv 2505.14172, arXiv 2410.19730), and another study (CharBench, arXiv 2508.02591) finds it only weakly related to correctness, with word length and the true count mattering more. The cause is debated. The fix works whichever cause is right.
The fix is to run a script. Verified: ran this on macOS:
echo banana | grep -o n | wc -l
It printed 2 (the macOS wc pads with spaces; the number is 2). One preprint (arXiv 2410.14166, by Xu and Ma; its full text, not its abstract) reports that coding models asked to write Python for such counting tasks do them perfectly, while the same models fail when answering open-endedly. General practice: so for exact counts, have the model write the script and read the script and its output. Treat a count it states from “doing the sum in its head” as a guess to check.
The bioinformatics versions of the same trap:







You want
Give it to




Number of sequences in a FASTA
grep -c '>' file.fa (Verified: ran on a three-record mock file, printed 3), or seqkit stats


GC content, read length statistics
a script, run by the agent, with the code visible


A p-value or any test statistic
a stats library in a script you can read and re-run


Sum or mean of a column
awk, or a script that prints the number; a number stated in prose is a guess



Rule of thumb: ask for the command and its output, and treat a count stated in prose as a guess to check.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


It can run Bash (the shell command tool) and write scripts, so ask: “write and run a command for this, and show me both the command and its output.”


Same rule. Not checked: how reliable small local models are at this. General practice: assume they count about as poorly, and ask for a script.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
Other ways it fails









Failure mode
What it looks like
What to do
Quest




Hallucination
A confident statement that is false. For example a plausible DOI, gene ID or tool flag that does not exist
Allow “I don’t know”; ask for word-for-word quotes first; restrict to supplied documents; look up every ID in PubMed or Ensembl, or run the tool’s --help
Spot the Mirage


Sycophancy
Telling you what you want to hear. It agrees with your wrong hypothesis, or softens a correct criticism when you push back (Sharma et al., arXiv 2310.13548)
General practice: ask for the strongest case against your idea, and hold back your preferred answer
none yet


Long-context degradation
Accuracy and recall drop as input grows (“context rot”, per Anthropic’s docs: the longer the input, the worse the recall); relevant text in the middle is used less (arXiv 2307.03172)
Curate input: head, counts, filtered tables; start fresh for a new task
The Context Window


Instruction drift
An early instruction is forgotten, for example after compaction (the harness replacing old conversation with a summary to free room)
Short instructions file (CLAUDE.md or similar, loaded at session start); a hook for must-never rules (Claude Code)
The Context Window


Non-determinism
The same prompt can give different answers
Not checked in the official docs. General practice: run twice and compare; record command, model and version; treat the script it wrote as the reproducible part
Same Every Time


Overconfidence
Reports a task as done while it is unfinished, often because it had no way to check
Give it a check to run (tests, row counts, md5) and read the output
none yet


Prompt injection
Text from fetched content that the model treats as an instruction. For example a README, PDF or FASTA header contains instructions the agent follows
Treat fetched content as data; review commands before approving; no system is fully immune
Plug In a Server

Newer tool versions or database releases postdate its training
Check --version and the current docs. Current Claude models list a June 2026 cutoff

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
The decision rule
Can I check the result cheaply and independently? If yes, ask the model: a bad answer is likely to show (omissions may not, so check those deliberately). If the answer must be exactly right and cannot be checked, use a script.

Ask a model to count one letter in a long word (or a mock 40-letter DNA string), then check it with grep -o and wc -l. Note whether it was right, and how sure it sounded. One try is a demonstration and falls short of proof.


Have a model summarise a methods paragraph you wrote. Check every number, name and negation against your original, and note anything omitted.

A single Skill in your folder helps you. A plugin is a folder that bundles Skills, and optionally agents, hooks and MCP servers (add-on connections that give the agent extra tools), so a whole group can install the same set and get updates.

title: Bundle a Plugin
section: Installing one is a trust decision
text:
Installing one is a trust decision






Warning



Per the Claude Code docs, a plugin you install can run arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges. Hooks, monitors, local MCP and language servers, and anything in bin/ run outside the sandbox and the permission rules. Skills and agents enter the context as instructions, and instructions can steer the agent too.


Before installing or updating a plugin:

Check where it comes from. A marketplace name says who publishes it. Reading the plugin shows what it does.
Read hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, and anything in bin/. These are where code lives.
In a session, /plugin shows what will be installed. claude --plugin-dir <dir> plugin details <name> lists a component inventory without a session.
Remember that auto-update can change files you reviewed. Pin a version for plugins you publish.

title: Bundle a Plugin
text:
When a team shares Skills
Idea from the GitHub Blog article “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” by Andrea Griffiths (GitHub Blog), in our own words. It is advice for teams and sits outside the plugin format.

Keep project names and conventions in one file. The reference genome build, the sample-ID pattern and the results folder names belong in a single project-facts file (a plain file that lists them, separate from the plugin’s plugin.json) which every Skill reads, so no SKILL.md repeats them. Then another lab can reuse your Skills with its own file and no rewriting, and a rename touches one place.
Keep discovered details apart from team standards. A pattern the agent finds in your code is an observation. Store it separately, and have a person confirm it before it becomes a standard.
If you generate copies, check for drift. Say you keep one source SKILL.md and generate copies for other tools. Run a check in CI (automated checks that run on every change) that fails when a copy no longer matches its source.
Blocking a merge depends on repository rules and required checks. Whether a bad change is stopped depends on those rules. A review step written in a Skill is advice unless a required check backs it.


Turn the Skill you wrote into a plugin folder with a plugin.json, then run claude plugin validate on it and read the output.

Time: about 20 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code v2.1.323 and OpenCode docs (they describe V2; installed version not checked) on 2026-11-13 (sources in research/forest-and-reef.md and research/doctor.md).
An instructions file is read every session. A Skill is a procedure loaded only when it is relevant, so it can be long without crowding the context.

title: Forge a Skill
text:
What a Skill is
A Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file. Only each Skill’s short description is preloaded. The body is read when the Skill is used. A Skill can also bundle scripts and other files. In Claude Code, both you (by name, such as /check-fasta) and the agent (by matching the description) can start one.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Place it at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (project) or ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (all projects). All frontmatter fields (frontmatter: the settings block between the two --- lines at the top of the file) are optional, but write a clear description so it triggers at the right time. Keep the body under about 500 lines. The older .claude/commands/ format still works but is merged into Skills.


OpenCode reads skills from .opencode/skills, .claude/skills and .agents/skills, so the same SKILL.md can serve both tools. Custom agents live in .opencode/agents/*.md.



An example you can write by hand in a scratch folder:
---
name: check-fasta
description: Count the records in a FASTA file and find duplicate IDs. Use before running any analysis on a new FASTA.
---

1. Run `grep -c '>' FILE` to count records.
2. Run `grep '>' FILE | sort | uniq -d` to find duplicate IDs.
3. Report what you ran and its output. Leave FILE unchanged.

title: Forge a Skill
section: Do it: install it, then confirm it loaded
text:
Do it: install it, then confirm it loaded
Writing the file is half the job. A Skill with a typo in its frontmatter loads silently with no fields set, so always check.

In a scratch folder (never a real project), save the example above as .claude/skills/check-fasta/SKILL.md. The --- must be the very first line of the file.
Make a tiny test file: printf '>a\nACGT\n>a\nGGCC\n' > reads.fa (two records, one duplicated ID).
Confirm the tool can see it:


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Start claude in the scratch folder. Type / and look for check-fasta in the menu, or run /skills. If you created a top-level skills folder after the session started, run /reload-skills. Then ask in plain words, leaving the Skill unnamed: “I just got reads.fa from a collaborator. Is it OK to analyse?” The agent should load the Skill and report the commands it ran.


Start opencode in the scratch folder. OpenCode finds .claude/skills too. The model loads a Skill through its skill tool, and you can load one yourself by writing @check-fasta in a prompt. Then ask the same question and check whether the Skill was used.




If it did not trigger, check in this order: the file starts with --- on line 1; the YAML (the key: value text format used in that block) parses; field names are spelled right; the description says when to use it, with the key use case first (long descriptions are cut off in the listing).

A Skill that is listed but never picked up is a finding about the description or the prompt. Next you will learn to measure that.
If a Skill never fires, two slash commands (a /command typed inside the running tool) help you look. /skills lists the skills the tool can see, and t sorts them by token count (how many tokens, the chunks of text a model reads, each one takes). /skill-doctor (v2.1.252 or later) shows each skill’s context cost (how much of the model’s limited reading space its text takes up) and how often it is used, and flags skills that sit in the listing but are never invoked. It excludes bundled and enterprise skills.






Warning



In Claude Code, allowed-tools in a Skill pre-approves tools for that turn (one prompt and its reply). Other tools stay available to the agent. A Skill offers no sandbox, and a Skill you download is code you choose to trust. Read it before installing it, as you would read a script.

title: Forge a Skill
section: Design the Skill like a small job
text:
Design the Skill like a small job
Idea from the GitHub Blog article “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” by Andrea Griffiths (GitHub Blog). The points below are our own wording of its advice, and the Agent Skills standard itself is outside the article’s scope.

One Skill, one job. Give it a defined input (what it is handed, such as a FASTA path) and a defined output (what it must return, such as a count and a list of duplicate IDs). If you need “and also” in the description, you probably have two Skills.
Say what it does and when to use it. The name and description should state the task and its purpose. In the body, add a short When to use part, and a What evidence to report part (the commands run and their output), so a reviewer can see what happened.
Start from a task you keep explaining. If you re-explain the same check each session, such as how to confirm a FASTQ file has no truncated records, that check is your first Skill. Write down its inputs, its limits and what a reviewer needs to see.
A Skill describes the method. The tool that runs it still supplies the tools, credentials and permissions. A Skill that says “submit this to the cluster” brings no cluster account or allocation with it.
Know when a Skill is the wrong fit. Skills suit bounded, repeatable work such as a pre-submission checklist for a samplesheet. Work that needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail or permissions enforced from outside, such as a lab’s shared sample-tracking service, suits an application (a separate program with its own tests and access rules) better than instructions.

Portability. The Claude Code and OpenCode docs listed in Lore below say both read .claude/skills, so one SKILL.md can serve both. The article’s advice, which is a sensible habit, is to verify in each client (the tool that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or OpenCode) you use after installing: does it trigger on the right request, load the files the Skill refers to, use the tools it needs, and return the evidence you asked for? Clients differ in models, tools and permissions, so a Skill that works in one can fail in another.

Write a SKILL.md for one chore you repeat (checking an input, summarising a log). Make the description say when to use it.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Prerequisites: Close the Loop. Objective: read and write a small Claude Code eval case that checks a Skill is triggered, and know what running it costs. Time: about 20 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code v2.1.325 plugin-evals docs on 2026-11-13 (sources in research/forge.md). claude plugin eval was not run for this page.
Words used below. Grader: a check that marks a run pass or fail. Arm: one condition of the comparison (with the plugin, or without). Ablation: removing the thing to see what changes. Judge model: a second model that marks the answer. Baseline: the run without the change.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Where this works
claude plugin eval needs Claude Code v2.1.269 or later. It evaluates a plugin directory (a folder with .claude-plugin/plugin.json), so first turn your Skill into a small plugin; the next quest covers bundling in more detail. The example exercises/forge/fasta-tools in this repository already has the shape:
fasta-tools/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json
├── skills/check-fasta/SKILL.md
└── evals/skill-triggers/
    ├── prompt.md
    └── graders/skill-fired.md

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


The case is a prompt plus one or more graders. The prompt is written the way a user would ask, and leaves the Skill unnamed:
---
runs: 1
---
I just got a new FASTA file called reads.fa from a collaborator. Can you check it is OK before I start the analysis?
The grader is a free check on the transcript, with no model call. It passes if the Skill tool was invoked for check-fasta:
---
type: tool_used
tool: Skill
input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?check-fasta"'
---
The check-fasta skill should be used when the user asks to check a new FASTA file, without naming the skill.
Run it cheaply while you iterate, one case, one run, no baseline arm:
claude plugin eval . --case skill-triggers --runs 1 --ablation none
The full comparison runs each case three times by default, with the plugin (WITH) and without it (W/OUT), and reports the difference (Δ):
claude plugin eval . --max-cost-usd 2
--max-cost-usd stops the run at a ceiling. Results land in evals/results/<timestamp>/ with a report.html.


Last verified (docs): the pages read describe OpenCode skills and plugins but no equivalent of claude plugin eval. Treat that as unconfirmed. You can still do the same comparison by hand: run one prompt several times with the Skill folder present, several times with it moved away, and compare using a script that checks the output. A small local model is cheap to run this way, but it follows Skills less reliably, so expect noisier results.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Reading the result

Six grader types exist. Four are free and computed from the transcript or files (regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists). Two use a judge model and cost tokens (llm, baseline; the baseline grader type is a different thing from the baseline run). Graders come from these six types only.
In a two-arm run, tool_used: Skill is shown as an indicator and counts towards the score only when you set arm: both.
Δ near zero with the Skill not firing is usually a real finding: the description does not trigger on that phrasing. Change the description, not the grader.
Pair one result grader with one process grader. Use llm graders only for short output, with a concrete PASS/FAIL rubric.
Each run happens in an isolated child session (a separate session started just for that run) with only the plugin loaded, so personal settings, the instructions file and other plugins are absent. Behaviour in your own setup may differ from a pass there.
claude plugin validate checks that the files are well formed. Behaviour needs an eval.







Note



Running an eval is the same trust decision as loading the plugin with --plugin-dir. Hooks you did not write still run code. Safety needs a review of its own, which a passing eval does not replace.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Who checks the work
Idea from the GitHub Blog article “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” by Andrea Griffiths (GitHub Blog), in our own words. The grader and baseline method above comes from the Claude Code docs.

Use a separate verifier, a check done by something other than the agent that did the work. An agent that marks its own work gives a self-check. For a QC skill that edits a samplesheet, have a script or a person diff the changed file against the original, and make the verifier cite the lines it relied on.
Check the Skill in each client you use (the tool that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or OpenCode). Passing in one tool says little about another. After installing, confirm that the client triggers the Skill for the right task, loads its files, uses the tools it needs and returns the evidence you expect.
Instructions guide; tests and people verify. A line in a Skill saying “check your work” steers the agent. Tests, CI checks (continuous integration: automatic checks that run when code is pushed) and human review verify.


Run the cheap one-case command above on exercises/forge/fasta-tools with a cost ceiling, and open the report.html. Note whether the Skill fired.


Write an eval case for your own Skill from the previous quest: a prompt that leaves it unnamed, and one grader.

title: Write the Brief
text:
Prerequisites: Recruit the Beast. The Context Window is advised. Objective: write prompts that make output checkable, and manage the context window so the agent stays on task. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code v2.1.323 and OpenCode docs (they describe V2; installed version not checked) on 2026-11-13 (sources in research/forest-and-reef.md).
The first branch of the skill tree is the brief: what you tell the agent. A vague brief invites a plausible guess. A good brief names the file and the symptom, says what “done” looks like, and gives the agent a check it can run.
Two habits make the rest of this safer:

title: Write the Brief
section: A role line is not a substitute for a brief
text:
A role line is not a substitute for a brief
A common habit is to open with “You are a world-class bioinformatician.” The one study we read on this found that expert personas are not a free gain. In a 2026 preprint (Hu, Rostami and Thomason), personas tended to help tasks about tone, format, safety and preference. They tended to hurt tasks that rely on what the model already knows: on the MMLU knowledge benchmark, accuracy fell from 71.6% with no persona to 68.0% with the shortest persona tested. The authors say shorter personas reduce the damage but do not remove it, and longer ones helped the alignment tasks more, so no length was best for both.
What to take from it (our reading, general practice):

Put your effort into the brief: the file, the symptom, what “done” looks like, and a check. Those are testable. A role line is not.
Use a role or tone line when you want a style, such as “explain this for a first-year student”, and not to make the model more accurate.
If you do use a persona on a factual task, test it against a version without one. See Close the Loop.

Limits: the study used small open models (7 to 8 billion parameters), not the large models you will likely use, and it is a preprint. It did not test flattery such as “world’s best”, so claims that flattery makes output worse go beyond what it shows.

title: Write the Brief
text:
Context is a budget
Everything in the conversation takes up room in the context window. The Claude Code docs note that old conversation can crowd out the files you need next.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


/context shows what is filling the window. /compact summarises the conversation (you can say what to keep). /clear starts fresh, which is right when you switch to an unrelated task. Claude Code also compacts automatically near the limit.


/compact (alias /summarize, meaning another name for the same command) summarises the session and /new (alias /clear) starts a new one. The docs show no /context equivalent in the TUI (the text user interface, OpenCode’s terminal screen).
