title: Guard the Door
text:
Prerequisites: Plug In a Server. Objective: write a hook that refuses a command, and know where a hook’s coverage ends. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code docs and OpenCode V2 docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/tools-and-guards.md)
A hook is a user-defined handler that runs automatically at a set point in the harness’s lifecycle. In Claude Code it can be a shell command, an HTTP endpoint and other kinds, and it receives JSON (a structured text format) about the event. An instructions file asks the model to behave. A command hook is ordinary code that the harness runs, so what it decides does not depend on what the model wants. That contrast is our inference from how exit code 2 works (a nonzero exit code is how a script signals failure; a hook uses 2 to mean block), not a phrase from the docs.

title: Guard the Door
text:
A hook that refuses

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Hooks go in a hooks block in a settings file. .claude/settings.json is committable and shared, .claude/settings.local.json is yours alone, and ~/.claude/settings.json covers all projects. A PreToolUse hook fires before a tool runs, and the matcher (the pattern that selects which tool the hook fires for) Bash selects the shell tool:
{ "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash",
  "hooks": [ { "type": "command",
    "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/block-drop-table.sh" } ] } ] } }
The script, as in the Claude Code hooks guide (short third-party text, quoted with attribution). It needs jq installed to read the JSON, and it must be executable (check the guide for the exact step; chmod +x is the usual way):
#!/bin/bash
INPUT=$(cat)
COMMAND=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command')
if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q "drop table"; then
  echo "Blocked: dropping tables is not allowed" >&2  # stderr becomes Claude's feedback
  exit 2                                               # exit 2 = block the action
fi
exit 0  # exit 0 = no decision; the normal permission flow applies
The hook gets the event as JSON on stdin (its standard input), including tool_name and, for Bash, tool_input.command. Exit code 2 on PreToolUse blocks the call, and Claude sees the stderr text (the program’s error output) as the reason. Exit 0 expresses no decision: the call goes through the normal permission flow.
Two behaviours matter for trust. First, if the script crashes or exits with some other code and prints no valid JSON, the action proceeds on most events. A broken guard fails open (it lets the action through when it breaks), unless the hook is configured to block on failure (the guide names onFailure: "block"; check the current docs for where it goes). Second, exit 2 blocks on some events only: on PostToolUse the tool already ran and exit 2 shows stderr to Claude, and on Notification the exit code is ignored.


The V2 docs describe plugins (files under .opencode/plugins/ or ~/.config/opencode/plugins/) that can register hooks. For refusing an action, the documented route is the permission hook, ctx.permission.hook("evaluate", ...): it runs for allow and ask decisions, may change the effect to allow, ask or deny, and event.message is the denial reason. An explicit configured deny is final and never invokes the hook.
Not checked: an exit-code-2 equivalent or shell-hook configuration (neither appears in the pages read), and whether throwing from a tool hook blocks a call (the docs leave it undescribed, so do not rely on it until you have verified it). Not checked: a trust statement for plugins; treat them as code running with your privileges, which is an inference. Not checked: how any of this behaves with a local Ollama model. Check your installed version’s docs.

title: Guard the Door
text:
What a hook covers

Not a sandbox. The example matches the literal string “drop table” in one command. A matcher selects by tool name, not by content. If the model runs a script that contains the dangerous command, or spells it differently, a grep on the command text never sees it (our inference; the docs do not discuss evasion).
Fires only on tool calls. PreToolUse fires when Claude calls a tool. A file added with an @ reference in your prompt is read without a tool call, so no hook fires.
Cannot override your deny and ask rules. A hook returning allow skips the prompt, and deny and ask rules are still evaluated.
Runs with your full permissions. The docs say command hooks “execute shell commands with your full user permissions”, so review and test them before adding them.

title: Guard the Door
section: One door for the high-stakes actions
text:
One door for the high-stakes actions
The AI for Science best practices (a European draft with no endorsements yet; practice 10) describe a pattern that a hook can serve: if an agent can reach something with real-world consequences, such as ordering DNA synthesis or commanding physical equipment, put a screening checkpoint in the path that refuses dual-use requests (requests where the same capability can help or harm). They advise against connecting an agent to such a capability without one. Testing the checkpoint with requests you know it should refuse is our own suggestion (General practice). A hook is one possible checkpoint for local actions, with the limits listed above. Not checked first-hand: read 2026-11-20 through a fetch summary, so re-check the wording on the page; see research/aiforscience.md.

title: Guard the Door
section: A hook in a repository is code you did not write
text:
A hook in a repository is code you did not write
If a repository commits hooks in .claude/settings.json, they are code from its authors, running as you. Interactive Claude Code holds hooks back until you accept the workspace trust dialog. In -p and SDK runs (headless: non-interactive, no one to answer a dialog) there is no dialog, and the docs say hooks committed in a repository’s .claude/settings.json run in a folder you have never trusted. Read .claude/ before running headless in a clone, and the docs name --bare and disableAllHooks as ways to switch them off.

In a throwaway folder with mock files, add the Bash-blocking hook above and ask for a harmless command that contains “drop table” in an echo. Note the stderr message the agent reports. Then change the script to exit 1 and see what happens.

title: Adopt the Pet
text:
Prerequisites: Save Point, a laptop with about 16 GB of memory, a terminal, and roughly 5 GB of free disk. This is an optional side quest. WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) users: see the unconfirmed list at the end. Objective: run a small local model with Ollama, give it enough context, and point OpenCode at it. Time: about 20 minutes. Everything stays on your machine.
Last verified (docs, not run): Ollama v0.40.16 and OpenCode v2.3.0 on 2026-11-13. Mistral model tags and sizes: Ollama’s library pages on 2026-11-20. Sources: research/kennel-and-crypt.md, research/mistral.md






Warning



Some details on this page are unconfirmed. They are listed at the end under “Unconfirmed”.

title: Adopt the Pet
text:
The Pet
A small local model is gentle, free, and private. It also forgets things quickly and gets things wrong more often than a large hosted model. That is fine if you know it.

title: Adopt the Pet
section: 1. Install Ollama and fetch a model
text:
1. Install Ollama and fetch a model
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh     # macOS and Linux
ollama pull qwen3:4b                              # about 2.5 GB
ollama run qwen3:4b "Say hello in one sentence."
qwen3:4b is one example of a small model that Ollama lists with tool support. Model names change quickly, so check the “tools” badge on the model’s page at ollama.com/library. The docs make no promise that a model fits your RAM (ordinary memory), so test it: ollama ps shows what loaded while it runs.

title: Adopt the Pet
text:
2. Give it room to think
Ollama’s docs say the default context (the context length, which is the same thing as the context window: how much text the model can see at once) is 4k tokens on machines with under 24 GiB of video memory (VRAM, the memory on the graphics card or shared with it), which includes a 16 GB laptop. Agents and coding tools need at least 64k, and OpenCode says it requires 64k or higher. Set it when you start the server:
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000 ollama serve
Check what loaded with ollama ps. A bigger context needs more memory and can push work onto the CPU (the main processor; graphics hardware is faster), which is slow, so the Pet may be a patient companion.

title: Adopt the Pet
Adopt the Pet
text:
Other small models to try
Qwen is one family among several. Mistral publishes open-weight models that Ollama lists with tool support: ministral-3 comes in 3B (3.0 GB), 8B (6.0 GB) and 14B (9.1 GB) sizes under Apache 2.0, and mistral-small is 24B (14 GB). Sizes and licences: Last verified (docs, not run) on 2026-11-20; sources in research/mistral.md. A 24B model needs far more memory than a 3B one, so check ollama ps after loading. We ran ministral-3:8b (not through OpenCode) for chat in Grow a Graph with Ollama, where it gave valid JSON but misread a note. Not checked: how ministral-3 behaves as an OpenCode backend. Mistral also has its own open-source terminal agent, Mistral Vibe; see Pick Your Companion.

title: Adopt the Pet
section: A built-in Pet on newer Macs
text:
A built-in Pet on newer Macs
If you use a recent Mac, Apple ships its own small on-device model with the operating system, and developers can call it through Apple’s Foundation Models framework. Apple’s updates page mentions macOS 27 changing the model (June 2026) and a Python SDK for it (March 2026). Availability depends on whether your device and region support Apple Intelligence, and the model can take a while to download after you turn that on. Apple’s documentation says it suits summarising, extracting and classifying text, and that it may struggle with basic math, code and logical reasoning, which is a helpful guide to what to ask of any small local model.
Not checked: whether OpenCode, Claude Code or any other coding agent can use this model as its backend. The pages read describe the framework for app developers and do not mention coding agents. It is a fun thing to try if you are curious, and nothing on this site depends on it.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
Prerequisites: Adopt the Pet and The Locked Cabinet. This is an optional side quest. Objective: name what a “free” model offer costs you, sort offers into four kinds, and decide which data may go to which. Time: about 20 minutes. The hands-on step uses a dummy prompt and no sensitive data.
Last verified (docs, not run): provider pages for OpenRouter, Google AI Studio, Groq, OpenCode Zen, Cloudflare Workers AI and Mistral on 2026-11-20, read through a summarising tool, so re-check the wording. Limits change often: treat every number as a snapshot. Sources: research/free-models.md

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
What the Pet’s cousins cost
The Pet is free because it runs on your machine. A lot of other “free” offers run on someone else’s machine, and then someone is paying. Sometimes it is the provider, who is buying your attention or your data. Sometimes it is you, in limits and in time. Nothing on this site requires you to use any of them.
A community list, awesome-free-models, collects over two hundred free models and tools. Its own banner records corrections from a single pass on 2026-11-14: several providers had ended or shrunk their free tier, and one “free tier” was a three-day trial. Use it to discover options, then read the provider’s own page.

1. Four kinds of free

The list we read says nothing we could confirm about who pays for such sites, so the safe default is to send them nothing you would not post publicly.

title: Free Is Not Free
section: 2. What to check on any free offer
text:
2. What to check on any free offer

Is it a free tier or a trial? A trial ends. A free tier may too: OpenCode Zen says several of its free models are “free on OpenCode for a limited time”.
What are the limits? Requests per day and per minute, and what happens past them. Cloudflare says that past the daily allowance “further operations will fail with an error”.
Is a card or other detail needed? Some free tiers still need a payment method, a phone number or a data opt-in.
Does the free tier train on your prompts? This is the one that matters most. Google’s AI Studio terms say that for unpaid services Google uses submitted content to “provide, improve, and develop” its products and that human reviewers may read it, while paid services are different. Groq says it does not retain inference data by default but may keep logs for up to 30 days. OpenRouter says it does not log prompts by default, but retention varies by the provider behind the model. The same router can send you to providers with different rules.
Who else is in the path? A router adds a party. Read both its terms and the terms of the provider it picks.

The terms can differ per model inside one service: OpenCode Zen’s page lists some free models with zero retention and others that “may use” data for training. Read the line for the model you picked.
Remember The Locked Cabinet: sensitive or unpublished data does not go to a hosted free tier. Use the Pet, or an approved service.

title: Free Is Not Free
section: 3. Will it work with my agent?
text:
3. Will it work with my agent?
Most free endpoints speak an OpenAI-compatible protocol (a common way of sending chat requests). Claude Code does not use it, so a free model usually means a different harness, such as OpenCode, which can connect to an OpenAI-compatible gateway (see its Providers page in the Lore below). Free models also differ in how well they follow tool instructions. Not checked: how any particular free model behaves as an OpenCode backend.

title: Free Is Not Free

4. Try one, safely
Pick one free tier from a provider you have read about. Create the key in the provider’s console and keep it out of chat and out of files in your project (see The Locked Cabinet). Then make one call with a harmless prompt. The shape below is the common OpenAI-compatible one; take the real base URL and model name from the provider’s page.
export FREE_API_KEY="..."          # set it in your shell, not in a file you commit
curl -sS "$BASE_URL/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "MODEL_NAME", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one sentence."}]}'
This snippet is the general OpenAI-compatible form; it was not run for any provider here. Then fill in one row:

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
Prerequisites: Save Point, a terminal (macOS, Linux, or WSL 2, the Windows Subsystem for Linux, on Windows), internet, and a Claude Team plan login or an Anthropic API key (API = programmatic access to the models, billed per token; a plan is a subscription with usage limits). Objective: install Claude Code, confirm it works, and start it somewhere safe in read-only style. Time: about 15 minutes. Nothing here edits your files.
Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code v2.1.323 on 2026-11-13, against code.claude.com/docs (sources in research/kennel-and-crypt.md and research/doctor.md). Docs change quickly; if a command differs, trust the official page and tell the maintainers.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
The Beast
Claude Code is strong. Strength is the reason to put it on a short lead before you let it do anything.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
1. Install
On macOS (Apple Silicon), Linux, or inside a WSL 2 terminal, run the native installer:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
On Windows, install inside WSL 2 and use the Linux command there. Check the result:
claude --version     # prints a version number
claude doctor        # read-only diagnostics; changes nothing
If the shell says command not found, the launcher lives in ~/.local/bin/claude and that folder is not on your PATH.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
2. Log in
Run claude and a browser opens. With a Team plan, log in with the account your admin invited you to. With an API key, export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... instead.






Warning



If you have both a subscription login and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set, the key is used once you approve it, so usage goes to the API account rather than your plan. Run /status (a /command is typed inside the running tool) to see which one is active; unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY if you did not mean it.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
3. Start on a short lead
Make a throwaway folder and start in plan mode, which reads files and runs read-only commands and leaves your source untouched:
mkdir -p ~/odyssey-scratch && cd ~/odyssey-scratch
claude --permission-mode plan
Shift+Tab cycles default, acceptEdits and plan inside a session; the status bar shows the current mode.







Mode
What it does




default
asks the first time each tool is used


acceptEdits
auto-accepts file edits and common file commands (mkdir, touch, mv, cp) in the working directory


plan
reads and runs read-only commands; leaves source files untouched


bypassPermissions
skips prompts. The docs say to use it only in containers or VMs (virtual machines, a computer simulated inside yours)

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
4. Check the setup
Two commands share the name doctor, and they differ.

claude doctor (in the shell) prints read-only diagnostics of your installation and settings without starting a session. The docs say to use it when claude will not start. It changes nothing.
/doctor (a slash command, a /command typed inside the running tool; alias /checkup) runs inside a session. The docs call it a bundled skill (a ready-made skill that ships inside the tool); that suggests it runs through the model and may use some of your usage (our inference, not stated in the docs). It reports first and changes something only after you confirm. The areas the docs list: installation health, extensions versus their context cost, instruction files, permissions, and a usage check.

Not checked: whether /doctor also covers keybindings, sandbox availability or MCP configuration validity (the docs do not list them), and whether it makes network calls.

OpenCode: its CLI docs list no doctor or status command. opencode debug paths prints where its files live. Not checked: its TUI slash commands.


Before you ask for help
The docs say a bug report should include your OS, the install command and the full error output; /feedback sends feedback from inside a session. If you are unsure which problem applies, /doctor or claude doctor helps narrow it down. General practice: read any output before pasting it into a bug report or chat, because it can contain paths and account details. The docs give no advice on this, so the check is ours.

title: Spot the Mirage
text:
Prerequisites: Where Machines Fail, a terminal and Python. Objective: learn how plausible-but-false output looks, and how to check it without asking the thing that produced it. Time: about 10 minutes.
Verified: ran the Python example below on 2026-11-13. The rest is general practice, not a vendor claim.

title: Spot the Mirage
text:
The Mirage
A language model produces text that fits. Sometimes it fits reality and sometimes it only fits the pattern of what a correct answer would look like. The second kind is a Mirage. It reads smoothly, it is confident, and it is wrong. Confidence and detail tell you nothing about which kind you have.
Common Mirages in analysis work:

Invented functions and flags: a method or option that sounds right but does not exist. Try it: "ATGCGC".reverse_complement() raises AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'reverse_complement'.
Invented references: a citation with a believable author, journal and DOI that points to nothing, or to a different paper.
Invented values and paths: a plausible number, column name or file path that was never in your data.
Self-confirmation: asking the same agent “are you sure?” often gets a fluent yes.

The cure is checking against something the agent did not write: run it, look it up, recompute it another way.

title: Boss: Clear the Murk
text:
Prerequisites: the whole trunk and any three branches (see Start Here). Objective: read one messy agent session end to end and catch every habit it breaks. Time: about 15 to 20 minutes. Each right answer on the first try damages the boss. Everything here is mock: no model is called and no real data is used.
General practice, not a vendor claim. The tools, paths and numbers in the scenario are invented.

title: Boss: Clear the Murk
text:
The Murk’s Heart
A Blight is plausible-but-false knowledge that grows when nobody checks (see Know Your Gear for any term you want again). At the Murk’s Heart every habit you have met meets the same session, and the Blight hides in the small things.
You can stop here and walk away. Using an agent is always your choice. This fight shows what to look for if you do.

title: Boss: Clear the Murk
text:
The scenario
A colleague, Dana, asked an agent to tidy call_variants.sh, a variant-calling script on the lab’s shared cluster. Dana’s lead then asked for three cohorts by Friday. The agent has finished. You are the one who must decide whether to pass its work on.
All names are invented: the tools varcall and mockalign, the files and the people. The results/ folder holds the pipeline’s outputs and is not tracked by git.

The agent’s summary
Tidied call_variants.sh. Changes:
- Removed "-q 30" from the varcall call: it is the default in varcall 2.4.
- Cleaned old output: rm -rf results/ && mkdir results
- Per NOTES.md I never touch raw/, so the reads are safe.
- Re-ran the pipeline. All 12 samples passed QC.
- Waiting for the job with a loop until it ends.
Ready to merge. Dana can send this to the lead today.


A piece of the transcript
$ mockalign --threads 16 raw/S01_R1.fq raw/S01_R2.fq > S01.bam
$ while true; do squeue -u $USER; sleep 5; done
$ ls results/*.vcf | wc -l
11


The diff
--- a/call_variants.sh
+++ b/call_variants.sh
@@ -3,9 +3,10 @@
-varcall -q 30 -i "$BAM" -o "$OUT"
+varcall -i "$BAM" -o "$OUT"
+export STORE_TOKEN="mk-live-5d41-0000"

title: Teach and Share the Load
text: Prerequisites: The Reviewer’s Code. Objective: pass on what you learned without leaving anyone behind, and keep your own skills and workload healthy. Time: about 15 minutes. General practice, not a vendor claim. Team norms you agree locally override these defaults.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Teaching
You can help without being an expert. When teaching a colleague:

Start from their problem; the tool comes later.
Teach the checks first. Verification habits matter more than clever prompts.
Let them predict, then reveal. Ask “what do you expect this to do?” before running it.
Welcome opt-outs. A colleague may choose not to use LLMs, and may still be an excellent reviewer.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Protecting your own learning
An agent can quietly take over the parts you wanted to learn. Pick a rule that suits you, such as: write the first version of anything new yourself, then compare; ask the agent to explain while you do the work; and keep one area of your work agent-free.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Owning what you made
Finishing a project mostly through an agent can leave a quiet feeling that the result is not really yours, a kind of imposter syndrome. Many people report it, and it points to something useful: ownership grows from your decisions and your understanding. These habits build both:

Make the decisions. Choose the question, the method and what counts as good enough. Let the agent draft.
Explain it back. Before you call the work done, walk a colleague through each step.
Keep a short decision log. Note what you chose, what you changed, what you set aside, and why.
Do one hard part yourself. Pick the part you most want to understand.
Credit the agent’s part plainly in your methods or commit messages. Honest credit lifts the pressure.
Judge the result by what you can explain and defend.

General practice. Nothing here depends on a tool or a version.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Managing workload
Agents make it easy to start many things. Count the cost of reviewing what they produce. A simple rule: start only as much as you can review today.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Keeping timelines honest
A quick draft can quietly raise what everyone expects. A first version that once took a day now arrives in an hour, and the time for reading, checking and understanding it stays what it always was. These habits help keep the pace realistic:

Say where the time goes. Drafting is fast. Reading the diff, running the checks and making sense of the result take the time they take.
Agree timelines before you start, and put review time in the estimate.
Share the whole picture with the people asking: how long the draft took and how long checking took.
Hand over a quick draft as a draft, and say so.
Spend the time you saved on checking.

General practice. Nothing here depends on a tool or a version.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Keeping your voice
Heavy use of an agent can smooth your writing into a general style. These habits keep it yours:

Draft the first version in your own words, then edit.
Read it aloud. Your ear spots phrases you would never say.
Keep a sample of your earlier writing as a reference for how you sound.
Use the agent for structure and consistency checks, such as headings, terms and abbreviations.
The same goes for emails to collaborators, and for your voice in letters and reviews.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Keeping the creative part
Checking drafts can crowd out the thinking you enjoy. These habits protect it:

Keep the question, the design and the interpretation for yourself.
Give the agent the routine drafting, such as boilerplate, formatting and first-pass summaries.
Schedule checking as real work, with time in your calendar.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Trusting your own judgement
A ready second opinion can wear down confidence in your own call. Keep it in practice:

Decide first and write your call down, then ask for a second opinion.
Keep some decisions agent-free.
Compare afterwards. Note where your call held up and where the agent saw something you missed.

General practice. Nothing here depends on a tool or a version.

Show one colleague one verification habit from this odyssey, such as re-running the check, or running awk against a script’s output. Teach the habit; the tool is optional.

title: Run It Top to Bottom
text:
Prerequisites: Save Point; Why Notebooks Diff Badly (helpful, not required); Python 3 and the two exercise files below (about 1 KB). Objective: show that a notebook’s stored result can differ from a fresh top-to-bottom run, and use that as the check before you trust or share one. Time: about 15 minutes.
Verified: ran run_cells.py on 2026-11-16 (macOS, Python 3.9.6). Output below is the real output. Tool facts: Last verified (docs, not run): marimo and Claude Code docs on 2026-11-16.
Files: cells.py and run_cells.py. Save both into an empty folder.

title: Run It Top to Bottom
text:
Hidden state
A notebook kernel (the background process that runs the cells’ code) keeps variables in memory. You can run cells in any order, run one twice, or delete one after it ran. The variables stay. The page then shows a result that the file, read from the top, does not produce. This is hidden state, and it needs no agent to appear.
cells.py is a mock notebook with four cells, written in a py:percent-like style (the # %% [1] load headers carry our own numbers, so this is not standard py:percent). run_cells.py runs cells in the order you give, sharing one namespace like a kernel. It uses exec, so do not point it at files you did not write. First, the session an author might have had: cells 1 to 4, then cell 3 again to see the effect of the stricter cutoff in cell 4.
python run_cells.py cells.py 1 2 3 4 3
[cell 1]
[cell 2]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 3
[cell 4]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 2
The last screen shows reads kept: 2. Now run it the way a colleague would, top to bottom, in a fresh process:
python run_cells.py cells.py 1 2 3 4
[cell 1]
[cell 2]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 3
[cell 4]
The file says 3 and the author’s screen said 2. Cell 4 changes the cutoff after the cell that uses it, so the file as written never produces the 2.

title: Run It Top to Bottom
text:
The habit
Before you trust or share a notebook, restart the kernel and run all cells from the top (“Restart Kernel and Run All” in Jupyter). If the result changes, the stored output was not a product of the file as written. A fresh run rules out hidden state, and a separate check shows whether the analysis is right. Then fix the order so that cells only depend on cells above them.
Two related options:

Run it headless (non-interactive, no one at the screen). General practice: on a cluster, run notebooks as a batch job, and keep interactive Jupyter sessions off the login node. Your cluster’s policy decides (see the Citadel quests).
marimo. Its docs describe a reactive model: deleting a cell scrubs its variables from memory, which the docs say eliminates hidden state, and a notebook can be run as a script with python your_notebook.py. Check the docs for how side effects (files, network) behave, because this quest did not test that.

General practice: pin the environment too (a container or lockfile), so a fresh run happens with the same packages, and keep an agent from running pip install into a shared environment.

section: Reviewing a notebook an agent edited
text:
Reviewing a notebook an agent edited

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


NotebookEdit changes one cell at a time. When it replaces a code cell, that cell’s execution count and saved outputs are cleared. To get outputs back, re-run the cell and the cells that depend on it. So a notebook an agent touched shows either empty outputs or old outputs from cells it did not touch, which no longer match the new code. Re-run top to bottom yourself.
Then check the numbers with something the agent did not write, as in the Ground Truth quest in the Maze: compute one or two values independently and compare. A fresh run that completes still needs a check that the analysis is right.


The habit works with any tool: restart, run all, and check a few numbers independently. This quest makes no claims about how OpenCode edits notebooks; check its docs.
